LACTOBACILLUS is a genus of Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic or microaerophilic, rod-shaped, non-spore-forming bacteria. Lactobacillus is the most common probiotic found in food such as yogurt, and it is diverse in its application to maintain human well-being. Some Lactobacillus species are used as starter cultures in industry for controlled fermentation in the production of wine, yogurt, cheese, sauerkraut, pickles, beer, cider, kimchi, cocoa, kefir, and other fermented foods.

LACTOBACILLUS ACIDOPHILUS is a species of gram positive bacteria in the genus Lactobacillus. L. acidophilus is a homofermentative, microaerophilic species, fermenting sugars into lactic acid. These strains are commercially used in many dairy products in the production of acidophilus-type yogurt.
LACTOBACILLUS DELBRUECKII SUBSP. BULGARICUS (until 2014 known as Lactobacillus bulgaricus) is the main bacteria used for the production of yogurt.
LACTOBACILLUS CASEI is a species of genus Lactobacillus found in the human urinary tract and mouth. The most common application of L. casei is industrial, specifically for dairy production.

LACTOBACILLUS HELVETICUS is a lactic-acid producing, rod-shaped bacterium of the genus Lactobacillus. It is most commonly used in the production of American Swiss cheese and Emmental cheese, but is also sometimes used in making other styles of cheese, such as Cheddar, Parmesan, Romano, provolone, and mozzarella.

LACTOBACILLUS REUTERI is a Gram-positive bacterium that naturally inhabits the gut of mammals and birds. Although L. reuteri occurs naturally in humans, it is not found in all individuals. Dietary supplementation can sustain high levels of it in those with deficiencies.
LACTOBACILLUS RHAMNOSUS sometimes is used in yogurt and dairy products such as fermented and unpasteurized milk and semi-hard cheese.
LACTIPLANTIBACILLUS is a genus of lactic acid bacteria
LACTIPLANTIBACILLUS PLANTARUM is a widespread member of the genus Lactiplantibacillus, commonly found in many fermented food products

BACILLUS COAGULANS is a lactic acid-forming bacterial species. B. coagulans is often marketed as Lactobacillus sporogenes or a 'sporeforming lactic acid bacterium' probiotic, but this is an outdated name due to taxonomic changes in 1939.

STREPTOCOCCUS THERMOPHILUS also known as Streptococcus salivarius subsp. thermophilus is a gram-positive bacterium, and a fermentative facultative anaerobe, of the viridans group. It is also classified as a lactic acid bacterium.

CELLULASE is any of several enzymes produced chiefly by fungi, bacteria, and protozoans that catalyze cellulolysis, the decomposition of cellulose and of some related polysaccharides. Cellulase is used for commercial food processing in coffee.

LACTASE is essential to the complete digestion of whole milk; it breaks down lactose, a sugar which gives milk its sweetness. Lactase is an enzyme that some people are unable to produce in their small intestine.[5] Without it they can't break down the natural lactose in milk. Lactase produced commercially can be extracted both from yeasts such as Kluyveromyces fragilis and Kluyveromyces lactis and from molds, such as Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus oryzae.

Β-GALACTOSIDASE is a glycoside hydrolase enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of β-galactosides into monosaccharides through the breaking of a glycosidic bond. β-galactosidase is important for the lactose intolerant community as it is responsible for making lactose-free milk and other dairy products. Many adult humans lack the lactase enzyme, which has the same function of beta-gal, so they are not able to properly digest dairy products. Beta-galactose is used in such dairy products as yogurt, sour cream, and some cheeses which are treated with the enzyme to break down any lactose before human consumption.

In commercial food processing, TRANSGLUTAMINASE is used to bond proteins together. It is produced by Streptoverticillium mobaraense fermentation in commercial quantities or extracted from animal blood.
Xylanase is any of a class of enzymes that degrade the linear polysaccharide xylan into xylose,[1] thus breaking down hemicellulose, one of the major components of plant cell walls.

BUTTER is a dairy product with high butterfat content which is solid when chilled and at room temperature in some regions, and liquid when warmed. It is made by churning fresh or fermented cream or milk to separate the butterfat from the buttermilk. It is generally used as a spread on plain or toasted bread products and a condiment on cooked vegetables, as well as in cooking, such as baking, sauce making, and pan frying.

All categories of butter are sold in both salted and unsalted forms. Either granular salt or a strong brine are added to salted butter during processing. In addition to enhanced flavor, the addition of salt acts as a preservative.

Fat-free half and half is a bit of a paradox from a US regulatory standpoint. Real "half and half" has a legal minimum milkfat content — the standards of identity for half-and-half fall under 21 CFR Part 131, and specifically §131.180 sets the minimum at 10.5% milkfat. So it's technically an imitation or substitute product.

"Crème fleurette" isn't a legally protected or defined term in French regulation and is used by dairy and food service professionals to designate a liquid fresh cream that has only undergone pasteurization.
"Half and half" is a US product — equal parts whole milk and light cream, legally required to be at least 10.5% milkfat (usually closer to 10.5–18%).
Under FDA standard of identity, 21 CFR §131.150: heavy cream is cream containing not less than 36 percent milkfat, and it must be pasteurized or ultra-pasteurized, with homogenization optional.

Whipping cream is a high-fat dairy product (typically 30–36% milk fat) that, when chilled and beaten, traps air to form soft or stiff peaks. It is lightly sweetened for desserts, holds its shape for piping, and adds a rich, velvety mouthfeel to mousses, ganaches, and sauces. Because of its lower fat content than heavy cream, it whips faster but is less stable over time.

SOUR CREAM is a dairy product obtained by fermenting regular cream with certain kinds of lactic acid bacteria. The bacterial culture, which is introduced either deliberately or naturally, sours and thickens the cream. Its name comes from the production of lactic acid by bacterial fermentation, which is called souring. Fat percentage is 18-20%.

Cultured sour cream is the standard, "real" sour cream — cream that's been fermented with bacterial cultures to develop its characteristic tang and thickness, as opposed to "acidified sour cream," which is soured artificially with food-grade acids instead of live cultures.

Smetana is a type of sour cream from Central and Eastern Europe. It is a dairy product produced by souring heavy cream. It is similar to crème fraîche (28% fat), but nowadays mainly sold with 9% to 36% milkfat content depending on the country. Its cooking properties are different from crème fraîche and the lighter sour creams sold in the US, which contain 12 to 16% butterfat. It is widely used in cooking and baking.

Crème fraîche is a dairy product, a soured cream, with a pH of approximately 4.5. It is soured with a bacterial culture. European labeling regulations disallow any ingredients other than cream and bacterial culture. Fat percentage is more than 30%

Babassu oil is a light, natural vegetable oil extracted from the seeds of the babassu palm tree (Orbignya phalerata), native to the Amazon rainforest region of Brazil. CAMELINA sativa is a flowering plant in the family Brassicaceae and is usually known in English as camelina. The crop is being researched due to its exceptionally high level (up to 45%) of omega-3 fatty acids, which is uncommon in vegetable sources.

COCOA BUTTER is a pale-yellow, edible vegetable fat extracted from the cocoa bean. Cocoa butter is a major ingredient in practically all types of chocolates (white chocolate, milk chocolate, and dark chocolate).

COCONUT OIL, or copra oil, is an edible oil extracted from the kernel or meat of mature coconuts harvested from the coconut palm (Cocos nucifera).
Olivenöl, auch Baumöl (von mittelhochdeutsch boumöl), ist ein Pflanzenöl aus dem Fruchtfleisch und aus dem Kern von Oliven, den Früchten des Ölbaums gewonnen wird.

Beware of a confusion between the generic name (rapeseed oil) and more specific oil varieties: colza oil and canola oil. Not all languages distinguish between the two. It seems that only the oils with a low erucic acid percentage are fit for humans. So the naming difference between rapeseed, colza and canola might just be a language issue.

Rapeseed (Brassica napus), also known as rape, or oilseed rape, is a bright-yellow flowering member of the family Brassicaceae, cultivated mainly for its oil-rich seed, which naturally contains appreciable amounts of erucic acid. Rapeseed is the third-largest source of vegetable oil and the second-largest source of protein meal in the world.

TEQUILA is a regional distilled beverage and type of alcoholic drink made from the blue agave plant, primarily in the area surrounding the city of Tequila
WINE is an alcoholic beverage made from fermented grapes.
SPARKLING WINE is a wine with significant levels of carbon dioxide in it, making it fizzy. Sparkling wine is usually either white or rosé, but there are examples of red sparkling wines.
WHITE WINE is a wine whose colour can be straw-yellow, yellow-green, or yellow-gold.
MUSCADET is a French white wine.

RED WINE is a type of wine made from dark-colored (black) grape varieties. The actual color of the wine can range from intense violet, typical of young wines, through to brick red for mature wines and brown for older red wines. The juice from most purple grapes is greenish-white, the red color coming from anthocyan pigments present in the skin of the grape
Sauternes is a French sweet wine from the Sauternais region of the Graves section in Bordeaux.
A ROSÉ is a type of wine that incorporates some of the color from the grape skins, but not enough to qualify it as a red wine.

Fortified wine is a wine to which a distilled spirit, usually brandy, is added. Many different styles of fortified wine have been developed, including Port, Sherry, Madeira, Marsala, Commandaria wine, and the aromatised wine Vermouth.

MADEIRA is a fortified wine made on the Portuguese Madeira Islands, off the coast of Africa. Madeira is produced in a variety of styles ranging from dry wines which can be consumed on their own as an aperitif to sweet wines usually consumed with dessert.
MARSALA is a wine, dry or sweet, produced in the region surrounding the Italian city of Marsala in Sicily.

PORT wine (also known as vinho do Porto, Porto, and usually simply port) is a Portuguese fortified wine produced with distilled grape spirits exclusively in the Douro Valley in the northern provinces of Portugal.

SHERRY is a fortified wine made from white grapes that are grown near the city of Jerez de la Frontera in Andalusia, Spain. Sherry is produced in a variety of styles made primarily from the Palomino grape, ranging from light versions similar to white table wines, such as Manzanilla and fino, to darker and heavier versions that have been allowed to oxidise as they age in barrel, such as Amontillado and oloroso.
BRANDY is a spirit produced by distilling wine. Brandy generally contains 35–60% alcohol by volume (70–120 US proof) and is typically consumed as an after-dinner digestif.

It is assumed that the translations of smoke are the same as cooking smoke.

Smoke is a collection of airborne solid and liquid particulates and gases emitted when a material undergoes combustion or pyrolysis, together with the quantity of air that is entrained or otherwise mixed into the mass. Smoke is sometimes used as a flavoring agent, and preservative for various foodstuffs. Smoking is the process of flavoring, browning, cooking, or preserving food by exposing it to smoke from burning or smoldering material, most often wood. Meat, fish, and lapsang souchong tea are often smoked.

FLÜSSIGRAUCH ist eine wasserlösliche gelb bis rote Flüssigkeit, die zum Würzen verwendet wird. Es wird als Ersatz für das Kochen mit Holzrauch verwendet und behält dabei einen ähnlichen Geschmack. Es kann zum Würzen von Fleisch oder Gemüse verwendet werden. Es wird in der Regel durch Konzentration des Rauchs aus Holz hergestellt, kann aber auch beliebige Lebensmittelzusatzstoffe enthalten.

LIQUID SMOKE is a water-soluble yellow to red liquid used for flavoring. It is used as a substitute for cooking with wood smoke while retaining a similar flavor. It can be used to flavor any meat or vegetable. It is generally made by concentrating the smoke from wood, but can contain any number of food additives.

EL HUMO LÍQUIDO es un líquido soluble en agua de color amarillo a rojo utilizado para dar sabor. Se utiliza como sustituto de la cocción con humo de madera manteniendo un sabor similar. Se puede utilizar para dar sabor a cualquier tipo de carne o vegetal. Generalmente se elabora concentrando el humo de la madera, pero puede contener cualquier cantidad de aditivos alimentarios.

LA FUMÉE LIQUIDE est un liquide soluble dans l'eau de couleur jaune à rouge utilisé pour aromatiser. Il est utilisé comme substitut de la cuisson au fumage du bois tout en conservant une saveur similaire. Il peut être utilisé pour aromatiser n'importe quelle viande ou légume. Il est généralement fabriqué en concentrant la fumée du bois, mais peut contenir n'importe quel nombre d'additifs alimentaires.

Sorghum originated in Africa thousands of years ago and remains a staple across Africa, Asia, and increasingly the Americas, prized for its drought tolerance. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a chewy texture similar to farro. It's ground into flour for gluten-free baking, popped like popcorn, brewed into beer, or cooked whole as a side grain or porridge. Nutritionally, it's rich in fiber, protein, and antioxidants, and being naturally gluten-free, it's a popular wheat alternative.

Triticale is a hybrid grain bred by crossing wheat and rye, first developed in the late 19th century and refined for commercial use in Europe through the 20th century. Its flour has an earthy, nutty flavor that combines wheat's mildness with rye's slight tanginess. It's used to make breads, pastas, and crackers, often blended with other flours for improved texture and rise. Nutritionally, whole-grain triticale flour is high in fiber, protein, and minerals like magnesium and iron, though it still contains gluten.

WHEAT is a grass widely cultivated for its seed.

Whole wheat grain (Triticum aestivum) is the raw, unprocessed wheat kernel — bran, germ, and endosperm all intact, unmilled. Cultivated for over 8,000 years since its Fertile Crescent origins, it's the source grain from which both atta and maida are later produced. Raw, it has a hard, chewy texture with an earthy, nutty taste; when cracked (dalia) or sprouted, it becomes softer and slightly sweet. Used for porridge, khichdi, upma, sprouted salads, or ground fresh into atta. Nutritionally, it's the most nutrient-dense wheat form — highest in fiber, iron, zinc, magnesium, and B-vitamins, since nothing has been removed.
Blé tendre entier ou froment, cru

Soft white wheat is a low-protein variety grown mainly in the Pacific Northwest, California, and parts of the Midwest, prized for its adaptability to temperate climates. It has a mild, delicate, slightly sweet flavor with a pale color. Its low gluten content makes it ideal for tender baked goods like cakes, pastries, crackers, and flatbreads rather than yeasted bread. Nutritionally, it's primarily a source of carbohydrates, with modest protein and fiber content, especially when refined.

Soft red winter wheat is grown primarily in the eastern and central United States, planted in fall and harvested in early summer to take advantage of its cold-hardiness. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor with a subtle reddish-brown hue in the whole grain. Its low protein and gluten content make it well-suited for cakes, pastries, crackers, and flatbreads rather than yeasted bread. Nutritionally, it's mainly a carbohydrate source, with modest protein and fiber, especially in its refined form.
Durum wheat (Triticum durum or Triticum turgidum subsp. durum) is a tetraploid species of wheat.

Hard red spring wheat is grown mainly in the northern U.S. Great Plains and Canada, planted in spring and harvested in fall due to the region's harsh winters. It has a robust, nutty, earthy flavor, generally considered slightly more pronounced than winter wheat varieties. Its very high protein and gluten content make it prized for artisan breads, bagels, and pizza dough that require strong structure and chew. Nutritionally, it's rich in protein, fiber, and B vitamins, especially when milled as whole grain.

Hard red winter wheat is grown extensively across the U.S. Great Plains, planted in fall and harvested in early summer, making it one of the most widely cultivated wheat classes in the world. It has a robust, slightly nutty, earthy flavor with more depth than white wheat varieties. Its high protein and gluten content make it a top choice for yeasted breads, as well as all-purpose and bread flours. Nutritionally, it's rich in protein, fiber, and B vitamins, especially when milled as whole grain.

Hard white wheat is a relatively modern variety, developed and popularized in the U.S. during the 20th century as a milder alternative to traditional red wheat. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor without the bitterness often found in red wheat varieties. Its high protein and gluten content make it well-suited for yeasted breads, while also working for pastries and tortillas. Nutritionally, it's a good source of protein, fiber, and B vitamins, particularly when milled as whole grain.
Durum wheat pre-cooked, whole grain, cooked, no added salt
Freekeh (sometimes spelled frikeh) or farik is a cereal food made from green durum wheat (Triticum turgidum var. durum) that is roasted and rubbed to create its flavour.

WHEAT GERM is a concentrated source of several essential nutrients, including vitamin E, folate (folic acid), phosphorus, thiamin, zinc, and magnesium, as well as essential fatty acids and fatty alcohols. It is a good source of fiber. Wheat germ can be added to protein shakes, casseroles, muffins, pancakes, cereals, yogurt, smoothies, cookies, and other goods.
Wheat gluten is a food made from gluten, the main protein of wheat.

Semolina is the coarse, purified wheat middlings of durum wheat mainly used in making pasta and couscous.

Suji (semolina) is a coarsely milled wheat product, made by grinding the hard endosperm of wheat (often durum wheat) into granular particles, with bran and germ largely removed — similar refinement to maida but coarser in texture. Used across the Mediterranean and South Asia for centuries, it has a mild, slightly nutty taste and a distinctive grainy, granular texture that gives dishes a light, fluffy bite. Used for upma, sheera/halwa, dosa batter, idli, pasta, and as a coating for frying. Nutritionally, it's calorie-dense with moderate protein, but low in fiber like maida, retaining few micronutrients from the removed bran and germ.

Bulgur is a parboiled wheat product made by steaming or boiling whole wheat kernels, drying them, then cracking them into coarse or fine granules. Originating in the Middle East/Mediterranean region thousands of years ago (a staple in Levantine and Turkish cuisine), it retains the bran and germ since it's made from whole wheat. It has a mild, nutty, slightly toasty taste and a light, fluffy texture once rehydrated. Used in tabbouleh, pilafs, soups, and as a quick-cooking rice substitute. Nutritionally, it's high in fiber and protein, with more iron, magnesium, and B-vitamins retained than refined flour, and a moderate glycemic index.

Hulled barley is a whole grain barley with only the inedible outer shell removed.
Pot barley is barley that has been processed to remove its fibrous outer hull but has not been polished.

Pearled barley is barley that has had its outer hull and bran layer removed through a polishing (pearling) process. This distinguishes it from "hulled barley," which only has the inedible outer hull removed and keeps the bran intact. Lower in fiber than hulled barley (since the bran is polished away). Good source of manganese, selenium, and B vitamins like niacin. Mild, nutty flavor with a pleasantly chewy, slightly sticky texture when cooked — it releases starch similarly to arborio rice, which is why it works well in risotto-style preparations.
Malt is germinated cereal grains that have been dried in a process known as "malting".

Buckwheat, despite its name, isn't a wheat relative at all—it's a fruit seed related to rhubarb, originating in Central Asia and cultivated in China for thousands of years before spreading through Europe and Russia. Its groats have an earthy, nutty flavor with a slight bitterness that deepens when toasted (as in kasha), and they're used whole, ground into flour, or sprouted in dishes ranging from soba noodles to porridge and pancakes. Naturally gluten-free, buckwheat is a good source of plant protein, fiber, magnesium, and manganese, plus rutin, an antioxidant linked to cardiovascular benefits.

Millet is an ancient cereal grain domesticated in East Asia and Africa thousands of years ago, historically a staple in China, India, and parts of Africa long before rice and wheat became dominant. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a light, fluffy texture when cooked, and a firmer, chewier bite when toasted first. It's naturally gluten-free and used in porridges, pilafs, flatbreads, and baked goods, offering a solid source of magnesium, phosphorus, fiber, and plant protein, along with antioxidants.

Bajra is one of India's oldest cultivated cereal grains, especially prominent in the arid and semi-arid regions of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana, and Maharashtra, where it thrives in low-rainfall, sandy soil conditions. The small, round grains range from pale yellow to grey, with an earthy, slightly nutty flavor. Bajra is traditionally ground into flour for rotis (bajra ki roti) and khichdi, or used whole in porridges, especially during winter months for its warming properties. Nutritionally, it's rich in fiber, iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, offers a good plant-protein source, and is naturally gluten-free—making it a staple in both everyday rural diets and gluten-free food formulations.

Samai, or little millet (Panicum sumatrense, syn. Panicum miliare), is one of India's oldest cultivated minor millets, traditionally grown in the rain-fed hills and plateaus of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha for over 5,000 years. Its small, round grains carry a mild, subtly nutty flavor and light, fluffy texture when cooked. Valued for its resilience in poor soil and low rainfall, it's traditionally used as a rice substitute—steamed, boiled into porridge (kanji), or ground into idli and dosa batters—and is popular during religious fasting periods. Nutritionally, samai is rich in dietary fiber, iron, and B vitamins, has a low glycemic index, and is naturally gluten-free, making it valued in diabetic-friendly and gluten-free diets.

Varagu, known in English as kodo millet, is another of India's ancient minor millets, cultivated for over 3,000 years primarily in the drier, hilly regions of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh. It's one of the hardiest millets, thriving in poor soils with minimal water, and is often grown as a famine-reserve or marginal-land crop. The small, round, reddish-brown grains have an earthy, mildly nutty flavor similar to other millets. Traditionally cooked like rice, ground into flour for flatbreads, or used in porridges and idli/dosa batters, it's also popular in fasting foods and diabetic-friendly diets. Nutritionally, kodo millet is notably high in dietary fiber and polyphenol antioxidants, a good source of iron and B vitamins, naturally gluten-free, and has one of the lowest glycemic indices among cereals.
be careful with the species Amaranthus, contains often the wrong translation.

Amaranth is an ancient pseudocereal native to Central and South America, prized by the Aztecs as a staple crop alongside corn and beans. It has an earthy, slightly peppery flavor with a distinctive sticky, porridge-like texture when cooked, and it pops like tiny popcorn when toasted dry in a hot pan. Naturally gluten-free, amaranth stands out for its unusually high protein content complete with lysine (an amino acid most grains lack), along with good levels of iron, magnesium, and calcium.

USDA NDB 20001 is a generic entry covering amaranth grain broadly (species like Amaranthus cruentus, hypochondriacus, or caudatus), not specifically black-seeded varieties. "Black amaranth" usually refers to darker-seeded cultivars (sometimes ornamental/wild types like Amaranthus hybridus), which can differ slightly in flavor (often described as more bitter/earthy than the common cream-colored grain amaranth) and are less commonly the ones used in commercial food products.

Native to Central and South America, amaranth was a staple grain of the Aztec and Inca civilizations, prized for its resilience and nutritional density. Black amaranth seeds have a mild, earthy, slightly peppery flavor with a subtle nuttiness that intensifies when toasted or popped. Versatile in the kitchen, they can be cooked like porridge, popped for snacking or garnishing, ground into flour for gluten-free baking, or sprouted for salads and bowls. Nutritionally, amaranth is a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, including lysine—rare among grains. It's also rich in fiber, iron, magnesium, and manganese, and naturally gluten-free, making it a nutrient-dense choice for ancient-grain and health-focused products.

Amaranth seed, pale brown (Amaranthus cruentus), known regionally as Rajagaro (Gujarati), Ramdana (Hindi), and Cavali biya (Marathi), among other local names. Unlike the deep black-seeded variety, this pale brown form has a milder, subtly sweet, nutty flavor. In Indian cuisine, it's commonly popped and used in fasting foods (vrat ka khana), ground into flour for flatbreads, or mixed with jaggery to make chikki-style sweets. Nutritionally, it's a good source of plant protein, dietary fiber, iron, and calcium, and is naturally gluten-free—making it a popular grain substitute during religious fasting periods across India.

Oats are a cereal grain that originated in Western Asia or Europe, historically used as animal fodder before rising to prominence as a hearty breakfast staple, especially in Scotland and Northern Europe. They have a mild, creamy, subtly sweet flavor with a soft, chewy texture that varies by processing—from firm steel-cut to quick-cooking rolled or instant forms. Oats are naturally gluten-free (though often cross-contaminated during processing) and are notable for their beta-glucan fiber, which supports heart health, along with solid amounts of protein, manganese, and iron.
Oats (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)

Rolled oats are whole oat groats that have been steamed and pressed flat with large rollers, a processing method developed in the late 1800s to shorten cooking time while keeping the grain mostly intact. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a soft, chewy texture that holds its shape better than instant oats, making them the classic choice for traditional oatmeal, granola, and baking. Like other oats, they're naturally gluten-free (if uncontaminated) and rich in beta-glucan fiber for heart health, plus protein, manganese, and iron, though their nutrition is nearly identical to whole oats since minimal processing preserves the bran and germ.

Quinoa is an ancient pseudocereal native to the Andean region of South America, cultivated by the Incas for thousands of years and revered as a sacred "mother grain." It has a light, slightly nutty and earthy flavor with a delicate crunch, and its grains form a small, curled tail when cooked that gives it a distinctive texture. Naturally gluten-free, quinoa is notable for being a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, and it's also a good source of fiber, iron, magnesium, and manganese.

Rye is a cereal grain native to Southwest Asia and Eastern Europe, historically thriving in cold, poor soils where wheat struggled, making it a staple grain across Northern and Eastern Europe and Scandinavia. It has a bold, earthy, slightly sour and tangy flavor with a dense, hearty texture, most familiar in dark rye bread, pumpernickel, and crispbreads. Rye contains gluten (though less than wheat) and is valued for its high fiber content, particularly soluble fiber that supports blood sugar control, along with good levels of manganese, phosphorus, and B vitamins.

Rye grain hails from Central and Eastern Europe and Western Asia, favored for its hardiness in cold, poor soils. It has an earthy, slightly sour, tangy flavor with subtle spice notes. It's most often milled into flour for dense breads like pumpernickel, used for crispbreads, or malted for whiskey and beer. Nutritionally, it's high in fiber and B vitamins, with a lower glycemic impact than wheat.

Medium rye flour is milled from whole rye with some bran sifted out, a grain long grown across Northern and Eastern Europe for its hardiness in cool climates. It has an earthy, slightly tangy flavor and a denser character than wheat flour. It's prized for European-style breads, sourdoughs, and crackers, though its lower gluten content means it's often blended with wheat flour or given longer fermentation for a good rise. Nutritionally, it offers more fiber, B vitamins, and minerals than refined wheat flour, with a gentler effect on blood sugar.

Spelt is an ancient wheat variety that originated in the Near East and was widely cultivated across Europe, particularly Germany and Switzerland, from the Bronze Age until being largely displaced by modern wheat. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a tender yet chewy texture, used much like wheat in bread, pasta, and baked goods, often prized for its more digestible protein structure. Spelt does contain gluten and offers a good source of fiber, protein, manganese, and B vitamins, along with more zinc and iron than common wheat.

Kamut (a trademarked name for Khorasan wheat) is an ancient grain with roots in the Fertile Crescent, popularized in the U.S. after seeds were reportedly brought over from Egypt in the mid-20th century, though its "King Tut's tomb" origin story is more legend than fact. It has a rich, buttery, nutty flavor with a firm, chewy texture, and its grains are notably large—up to twice the size of modern wheat kernels—making it popular in pastas, breads, and cereals. Kamut contains gluten but is prized for its higher protein and mineral content compared to common wheat, offering good levels of selenium, zinc, magnesium, and antioxidants.

Teff is a tiny ancient grain native to Ethiopia and Eritrea, where it has been cultivated for thousands of years and remains a dietary staple, most famously as the base for injera flatbread. Despite its small size, it has a rich, slightly sweet, nutty, almost molasses-like flavor. It's typically ground into flour for fermented flatbreads and porridges, or cooked whole as a side grain similar to quinoa. Nutritionally, it's naturally gluten-free and notably high in iron, calcium, and fiber compared to most other grains.
FLOUR is a powder made by grinding raw grains or roots and used to make many different foods.
Farine de blé tendre ou froment T110
IFCT classifies by processing description, while the French system is a legally defined ash-content standard — so the mapping is functional/nutritional rather than an exact technical equivalence.

Wheat flour comes from wheat, one of the world's oldest cultivated grains, first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent around 10,000 years ago and now the dominant grain in global bread-making, especially in Europe, the Middle East, and the Americas. It has a mild, slightly sweet, neutral flavor with a texture that ranges from soft and fine (cake flour) to coarse and hearty (whole wheat), largely defined by its protein and gluten content, which gives dough its characteristic elasticity and chew. Wheat flour contains gluten and, depending on whether it's whole grain or refined, provides varying levels of fiber, B vitamins, iron, and protein—whole wheat retaining significantly more nutrients since the bran and germ aren't stripped away.
In France, "Wheat, flour, refined" (maida) corresponds most closely to farine de blé type 45 (T45), and to a lesser extent type 55 (T55).

Maida is a highly refined wheat flour, milled from Triticum aestivum after the bran and germ are removed, leaving mostly starchy endosperm — a process that became widespread in India with industrial roller-milling. It has a mild, slightly sweet, neutral taste, making it a versatile base that readily takes on other flavors. Maida is used for naan, bhatura, puri, pastries, cakes, biscuits, and samosa wrappers, prized for its soft, elastic texture. Nutritionally, it's calorie-dense (~348 kcal/100g) but low in fiber and micronutrients (iron, zinc, B-vitamins), with a high glycemic index compared to whole wheat flour.
Farine de blé tendre ou froment T55 (pour pains)
Farine de blé tendre ou froment T65
Wheat flour, whole-grain (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)

Soft wheat has been cultivated for millennia, with whole-grain flour production expanding globally as milling techniques evolved to preserve the bran and germ. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor that's less robust than hard wheat varieties. Its lower protein and gluten content make it ideal for tender baked goods like cakes, pastries, cookies, and flatbreads rather than yeasted bread. Nutritionally, it retains more fiber, B vitamins, and minerals than refined flour, thanks to the whole grain remaining intact.
Farine de blé tendre ou froment T150
Indian atta (whole wheat flour, IFCT A013) would map to T150 ("farine intégrale") or sometimes T110, since these retain most or all of the bran and germ.

Atta is whole wheat flour, stone-ground or milled from Triticum aestivum using the entire grain — bran, germ, and endosperm intact. This traditional chakki-milling method has been used across South Asia for centuries, predating industrial refining. Atta has a warm, nutty, slightly earthy taste with a denser, coarser texture than refined flour. It's the staple for everyday Indian breads — roti, chapati, paratha — and is also used in some baked goods. Nutritionally, it's rich in fiber, iron, magnesium, and B-vitamins (retained from the bran and germ), with a lower glycemic index than maida, making it more filling and slower-digesting.
Farine de blé tendre ou froment T110

Barley flour or meal is made by grinding whole or pearled barley grains into a fine (flour) or coarse (meal) powder. Good source of dietary fiber, especially beta-glucan (a soluble fiber linked to cholesterol and blood sugar benefits), provides B vitamins, selenium, and manganese.
Maronenmehl wird aus getrockneten und geschälten Kastanien hergestellt und meist mehrfach gemahlen.
Chestnuts can be dried and milled into flour, which can then be used to prepare breads, cakes, pies, pancakes, pastas, polenta, or used as thickener for stews, soups, and sauces.

Blue corn flour is a stone-ground flour made from whole kernels of blue (or purple) corn — a corn variety, distinct from standard yellow or white corn, that owes its color to natural anthocyanin pigments (the same class of antioxidant compounds found in blueberries and purple cabbage). it's generally comparable to other whole-grain corn flours in calories and carbohydrates, but the anthocyanin content gives it additional antioxidant properties and a naturally sweeter, nuttier flavor than yellow corn flour.
Corn flour, whole-grain, blue (harina de maiz morado)

White corn flour is a flour ground from the whole kernel of white corn — a corn variety that lacks the yellow/orange carotenoid pigments found in standard yellow corn. it's very similar to whole-grain yellow corn flour in calories, protein, and fiber — the main practical difference is the near-absence of vitamin A precursors.

Yellow corn flour is flour ground from the whole kernel of yellow corn, the most common corn type used in the US. Yellow corn gets its color from carotenoids, including beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A — so unlike white corn flour, yellow corn flour has some vitamin A activity.
Rice flour is a form of flour made from finely milled rice.

Corn flour comes from maize, a grain domesticated in southern Mexico around 9,000 years ago and later becoming a dietary cornerstone across the Americas, from Mexican tortillas to Southern U.S. cornbread. It has a mild, slightly sweet, distinctly corn flavor with a fine, slightly gritty texture that lends baked goods a tender crumb and golden color. Naturally gluten-free, corn flour offers decent fiber and is a good source of B vitamins and antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin, though its protein is incomplete and lower in quality compared to grains like quinoa.

Native to Mesoamerica and introduced to India centuries ago, tender local maize (Zea mays) refers to indigenous Indian corn varieties harvested young, while the kernels are still soft and milky rather than fully mature and dried. It has a starchy, mildly sweet, earthy flavor—less sugary than sweet corn but with a satisfying bite. Widely enjoyed as street food, it's traditionally roasted over open coals and rubbed with lime, chili, and salt (bhutta), boiled as a snack, or grated into curries, soups, and flatbreads. Nutritionally, tender maize provides dietary fiber, complex carbohydrates, and moderate protein, along with B vitamins, magnesium, and antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin, making it a wholesome seasonal staple across India.

White corn is from the whole kernel of white corn — a corn variety that lacks the yellow/orange carotenoid pigments found in standard yellow corn. it's very similar to whole-grain yellow corn flour in calories, protein, and fiber — the main practical difference is the near-absence of vitamin A precursors.

Yellow corn is from the whole kernel of yellow corn, the most common corn type used in the US. Yellow corn gets its color from carotenoids, including beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A — so unlike white corn flour, yellow corn flour has some vitamin A activity.

Sweet corn is a cultivar of maize (Zea mays var. saccharata) bred to accumulate higher natural sugar content, harvested young and tender before the kernels mature and starch fully develops. Compared to local field maize, it has a distinctly sweeter, juicier taste with a crisp, tender bite. Popular worldwide, sweet corn is boiled or steamed on the cob, grilled, or used kernel-off-cob in salads, soups, stir-fries, and Indian street snacks like corn chaat. Nutritionally, it offers dietary fiber, carbohydrates, and moderate protein, along with vitamin C, B vitamins (especially folate), magnesium, and antioxidants such as lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health. Its natural sweetness also makes it a favorite in both savory and lightly sweetened preparations.

Rice is a cereal grain domesticated independently in China and possibly India thousands of years ago, and it remains the staple food for over half the world's population, central to cuisines across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. It has a mild, subtly sweet flavor with a texture that varies widely by variety—from the fluffy separate grains of basmati to the sticky clumps of short-grain sushi rice. Naturally gluten-free, rice's nutrition depends heavily on processing: brown rice retains its bran and germ for fiber, B vitamins, magnesium, and manganese, while white rice is more refined and comparatively lower in nutrients.

Red rice is a whole-grain rice variety that gets its reddish-brown hue from anthocyanin pigments in its bran layer, with well-known types grown in regions like Thailand, Bhutan, and the Camargue in France. It has a robust, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a chewy, hearty texture, since the bran layer is left intact rather than polished away as with white rice. Naturally gluten-free, red rice is notably richer in fiber, antioxidants, and minerals like iron and magnesium than white rice, thanks to that retained bran layer.

CARNAROLI is a medium-grained rice grown in the Pavia, Novara and Vercelli provinces of northern Italy. Carnaroli is used for making risotto, differing from the more common arborio rice due to its higher starch content and firmer texture, as well as having a longer grain.

Generic sugar is vegan:maybe because some cane sugar is refined using bone char (charred cattle bones) as a decolorizing filter. This is primarily a North American practice. Beet sugar, organic sugar, and unrefined sugars never use bone char. Vegetarian status remains yes as bone char is a processing aid and the final product contains no animal-derived material.

Sugar (sucrose) comes from sugarcane, first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years ago and later spread through Asia and the Middle East to become the dominant global source, and from sugar beet, which took hold in Europe after Napoleon's early 1800s Continental Blockade cut off cane sugar imports and spurred domestic beet production, making it the region's primary source today. It has a pure, intensely sweet flavor with no notable aroma, available in forms ranging from fine granulated and powdered sugar to coarser raw and brown sugars with mild molasses notes. Used universally in baking, cooking, preserving, and sweetening beverages, sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, making it a source of energy without nutritional value.

Brown sugar is sugar—typically from sugarcane—that retains or has molasses added back in during processing, a practice with roots in unrefined "raw" sugars historically produced across the Caribbean, South Asia, and other cane-growing regions before fully refined white sugar became standard. It has a rich, warm, caramel-like flavor with subtle toffee and mineral notes from the molasses, and a moist, clumping texture ranging from light to dark depending on molasses content. Commonly used in baking, glazes, and sauces for its depth and moisture, brown sugar offers only trace minerals like calcium and iron from the molasses, making it nutritionally almost identical to white sugar—still primarily empty calories.

Invert sugar is a liquid sugar syrup produced by splitting sucrose into its component parts—glucose and fructose—through hydrolysis using heat, acid, or enzymes, a process discovered in the 19th century and now widely used in food manufacturing rather than home kitchens. It has a flavor sweeter than regular sugar (since fructose tastes sweeter than sucrose) with a smooth, syrupy texture, and it's prized in baking and confectionery for resisting crystallization, retaining moisture, and extending shelf life in products like candies, jams, and soft baked goods. Like other sugars, invert sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, offering energy without nutritional value.

Vanilla sugar is granulated sugar infused or blended with vanilla flavor—either from real vanilla beans/extract or artificial vanillin—a tradition especially popular in European baking, particularly in Germany, Scandinavia, and Central Europe, where small sachets are a pantry staple. It has a sweet flavor layered with warm, floral, slightly woody vanilla notes, and a texture identical to regular granulated sugar. Commonly stirred into batters, whipped cream, custards, and beverages for a quick flavor boost, vanilla sugar offers no meaningful nutritional value beyond what plain sugar provides—purely empty calories with trace aromatic compounds.
"granulated sugar" is generally white sugar, but other sugars can be in granulated form too.
Granulated, familiar as table sugar, with a grain size about 0.5-0.6 mm across.
Caster sugar is finer than granulated sugar, but coarser than powdered/icing sugar, with a grain size of about 0.35 mm.

Since the 6th century BC, cane sugar producers have crushed the harvested vegetable material from sugarcane in order to collect and filter the juice. They then treat the liquid (often with lime (calcium oxide)) to remove impurities and then neutralize it. Boiling the juice then allows the sediment to settle to the bottom for dredging out, while the scum rises to the surface for skimming off.

COCONUT SUGAR is a palm sugar produced from the sap of the flower bud stem of the coconut palm. It is used in savory dishes, but mainly in local desserts and cakes of the Southeast Asian region. Coconut sugar is subtly sweet almost like brown sugar but with a slight hint of caramel. The flavor and sweetness is usually similar to table sugar or brown sugar. There is no scientific evidence that coconut sugar is more nutritious or healthier than any other sweetener.

MALTOSE, also known as maltobiose or malt sugar, is a disaccharide formed from two units of glucose joined. Maltose is a component of malt, a substance which is obtained in the process of allowing grain to soften in water and germinate. It is also present in highly variable quantities in partially hydrolysed starch products like maltodextrin, corn syrup and acid-thinned starch. In humans, maltose is broken down by various maltase enzymes, providing two glucose molecules which can be further processed: either broken down to provide energy, or stored as glycogen. The lack of the sucrase-isomaltase enzyme in humans causes sucrose intolerance.

Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose, occurring naturally in many plants but concentrated commercially from sugarcane and sugar beet—the two primary sources refined into the table sugar found worldwide. It has a pure, intensely sweet flavor with no notable aroma, forming the chemical basis for the many refined sugar products (granulated, powdered, brown, etc.) that vary mainly in processing rather than composition. Used universally as a sweetener in food and beverages, sucrose provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, serving as a source of energy without nutritional value.
Molasses (American English) or black treacle (British English) is a viscous product resulting from refining sugarcane or sugar beets into sugar.

Trehalose is a naturally occurring disaccharide made of two glucose molecules, found in trace amounts in mushrooms, honey, and various plants and insects, and produced commercially today mainly through enzymatic conversion of starch, largely pioneered by Japanese researchers in the 1990s who made large-scale production affordable. It has a mild sweetness—roughly 45% as sweet as sucrose—with no notable aroma, and is valued in food processing for its exceptional stability, ability to protect texture and moisture in frozen or dried foods, and resistance to browning at high heat. Used in baked goods, frozen desserts, and dried fruits as a stabilizer and mild sweetener, trehalose provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, though it's digested more slowly than sucrose, giving it a gentler effect on blood sugar.

Melado is an unrefined liquid sugar syrup made from concentrated sugarcane juice, a traditional product especially common in Brazil and other Latin American countries where it's produced as a byproduct or lighter-processed cousin of molasses, retaining more of the cane's natural sweetness. It has a rich, deep caramel flavor with molasses-like notes but milder and less bitter than true molasses, and a thick, syrupy texture. Used in traditional desserts, sauces, and as a spread or sweetener in Brazilian and Latin American cooking, melado retains modest amounts of minerals like calcium, iron, and potassium from the cane juice, making it slightly more nutritious than fully refined sugar.

SYRUP is a condiment that is a thick, viscous liquid consisting primarily of a solution of sugar in water, containing a large amount of dissolved sugars but showing little tendency to deposit crystals.

Glucose is a simple sugar (monosaccharide) that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and plants, and is produced commercially by breaking down starch—typically from corn in the U.S. or wheat and potatoes in Europe—through enzymatic or acid hydrolysis. It has a moderately sweet flavor, less sweet than sucrose or fructose, with no notable aroma, and is available as a syrup or dried/powdered form used widely in candy-making, baking, and brewing for its resistance to crystallization and browning properties. As the primary fuel source for the human body, glucose provides purely caloric energy with no fiber, vitamins, or minerals, and it's the sugar that directly raises blood glucose levels, giving it the highest glycemic index among common sugars.

Fructose is a simple sugar (monosaccharide) that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and some vegetables, and is produced commercially either by processing corn starch into high-fructose corn syrup (mainly in the U.S.) or by refining it from sucrose. It has the sweetest taste of all natural sugars—notably sweeter than sucrose or glucose—with no notable aroma, and is used in beverages, baked goods, and processed foods both for its intense sweetness and its ability to enhance flavor and browning. Fructose provides purely empty calories with no fiber, vitamins, or minerals, and is metabolized differently than glucose—processed primarily by the liver—which has made it a focus of concern around excessive consumption and links to metabolic issues.
The wikidata names are not used on packages.

Oligofructose is a type of fructan—a short-chain fructose oligosaccharide—found naturally in plants like chicory root, onions, and bananas, and produced commercially mainly through partial enzymatic hydrolysis of chicory inulin, a process developed in Europe where chicory-based fibers are widely used. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 30-50% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and no notable aroma, and is used in food products as a low-calorie sweetener, fat replacer, and texture enhancer. Unlike simple sugars, oligofructose acts as a soluble prebiotic fiber that resists digestion in the small intestine and ferments in the colon, feeding beneficial gut bacteria while providing fewer calories than sucrose and supporting digestive health.

High-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) (also called glucose-fructose, isoglucose and glucose-fructose syrup) is a sweetener made from corn starch
Light syrup is similar to Golden Syrup, but is made slightly differently and is a bit thinner.
Dark syrup is similar to a mix of golden syrup and black treacle, being thinner and with a less pronounced flavour than that of black treacle.

Agave syrup (or agave nectar) is a liquid sweetener extracted from the core of the agave plant, particularly Agave tequilana, with production centered in Mexico where the plant has long been used to make traditional sweeteners and beverages like pulque. It has a mild, neutral sweetness—often noted as sweeter than honey—with subtle caramel notes in darker varieties, and a thin, smooth, honey-like texture that dissolves easily in cold liquids. Popular as a vegan honey substitute in beverages, baking, and dressings, agave syrup is very high in fructose (often 70-90%), giving it a low glycemic index despite being calorie-dense, though its fructose concentration has raised similar metabolic concerns as high-fructose corn syrup.

Isomaltooligosaccharide (IMO) is a short-chain carbohydrate composed of glucose units linked in branched α-1,6 bonds, found in trace amounts in fermented foods like miso, soy sauce, and sake, and produced commercially through enzymatic conversion of starch, a technology pioneered and widely commercialized in Japan since the 1980s. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 40-60% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and syrupy texture similar to corn syrup, making it a popular sugar substitute in protein bars, baked goods, and "low-sugar" products. Marketed as a prebiotic fiber that partially resists digestion and supports gut bacteria, IMO provides fewer calories than sucrose, though recent research has questioned how much of it is truly fermented in the colon versus digested as regular glucose, making its fiber and metabolic benefits somewhat contested.

Fructooligosaccharide (FOS) is a short-chain fructan found naturally in foods like chicory root, onions, garlic, and bananas, and produced commercially either by extracting it from chicory or through enzymatic conversion of sucrose, with much of the technology developed in Japan and France. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 30-50% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and no notable aroma, and is used in food products as a low-calorie sweetener, texture enhancer, and fat replacer. Like oligofructose, FOS acts as a soluble prebiotic fiber that resists digestion in the small intestine and ferments in the colon to feed beneficial gut bacteria, providing fewer calories than sucrose while supporting digestive health.

Protein is a macronutrient made of amino acid chains, sourced from a wide range of foods—animal sources like meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, and plant sources like legumes, grains, nuts, and soy—with humans relying on food-derived protein since prehistoric times as one of the three core macronutrients alongside fats and carbohydrates. Its flavor and texture vary enormously by source, from the rich, savory taste of meats to the neutral, often bland profile of isolated protein powders, which are typically processed from whey, soy, or pea into fine, mixable forms. Essential for building and repairing muscle, enzymes, and hormones, protein is measured by its amino acid completeness—animal proteins and a few plant sources like quinoa and soy are "complete," containing all nine essential amino acids, while most other plant proteins must be combined to achieve the same profile.

Hydrolyzed vegetable protein (HVP) is a flavor enhancer made by chemically breaking down plant proteins—typically soy, corn, or wheat—using acid hydrolysis, a process developed in the early 20th century and widely adopted in industrial food manufacturing to create savory, meat-like flavors without meat. It has an intensely savory, umami-rich flavor with notes reminiscent of broth or bouillon, and comes as a fine powder or paste used in tiny quantities to boost taste. Commonly used in soups, sauces, snack seasonings, and processed foods as a cheaper alternative to natural flavor development, HVP contributes free glutamic acid (similar to MSG) along with trace amino acids, but is used in such small amounts that it offers negligible nutritional value beyond flavor enhancement.

WHEY PROTEIN is a mixture of globular proteins isolated from whey, the liquid material created as a by-product of cheese production.

Casein is the primary protein found in milk, making up about 80% of milk's protein content, and has been used for centuries in cheese-making across dairy-producing regions worldwide, since it's the protein that coagulates to form curds. It has a neutral, mildly milky flavor with no strong aroma, and forms a thick, slow-digesting texture when consumed—clumping into a gel in the stomach, unlike whey which stays liquid. Widely used in cheese production and as a slow-release protein supplement (particularly popular before bed among athletes), casein is a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with calcium and phosphorus from its dairy origin.

Caseinate is a soluble form of casein—typically sodium or calcium caseinate—created by treating milk casein with an alkali to make it water-soluble, a processing method developed in the early-to-mid 20th century to allow casein's functional properties to be used more easily in manufactured foods. It has a neutral, mildly milky flavor with no strong aroma, and unlike regular casein, it dissolves smoothly in liquids and forms stable emulsions rather than clumping into curds. Widely used as an emulsifier and protein fortifier in coffee creamers, processed cheeses, and protein supplements, caseinate remains a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with calcium and phosphorus from its dairy origin.

Cocoa comes from the seeds (beans) of the cacao tree, native to Central and South America and used by the Aztecs and Maya for thousands of years in ceremonial and medicinal drinks long before it spread to Europe in the 16th century and became the basis for modern chocolate. It has a rich, bitter, complex flavor with earthy, fruity, and slightly astringent notes that vary by origin and processing, and comes in forms ranging from raw beans and nibs to fine cocoa powder, defined by its fat content (cocoa butter) after pressing. Used in chocolate-making, baking, and beverages, cocoa is notably rich in flavanol antioxidants, along with magnesium, iron, and fiber, though its bitter compounds are often offset with added sugar in most commercial products.

WHITE CHOCOLATE is made of sugar, milk, and cocoa butter, without the cocoa solids. It is pale ivory colour, and lacks many of the compounds found in milk and dark chocolates.

Water is a naturally occurring compound of hydrogen and oxygen, found throughout the environment in oceans, rivers, lakes, and groundwater, and sourced for consumption from municipal supplies, wells, springs, and glaciers depending on region. It has a neutral, essentially flavorless and odorless profile, though mineral content can lend subtle differences—spring water often tastes slightly mineral-rich, while distilled water tastes notably flat. As the foundation of virtually all food and beverage preparation, water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, though mineral or spring varieties may carry trace amounts of minerals like calcium, magnesium, and potassium, and it remains essential for nearly every bodily function.

Brewing water is water specifically treated or selected for beer or coffee production, with mineral content—calcium, magnesium, sulfate, chloride, and bicarbonate—carefully adjusted to match regional styles, a practice tracing back to historic brewing centers like Burton-on-Trent (high sulfate, favoring hoppy pale ales) and Pilsen (very soft water, ideal for delicate lagers). It has a neutral base flavor, but its mineral balance subtly shapes the final beverage's taste—sulfate accentuates hop bitterness and dryness, while chloride enhances malt sweetness and mouthfeel. Used as the primary ingredient in brewing (making up roughly 90-95% of beer), water's mineral profile is often adjusted through filtration, dilution, or targeted mineral additions to achieve consistency and match desired beer or coffee styles. As with plain water, brewing water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, only trace minerals that influence flavor rather than nutrition.

Carbonated water is water infused with dissolved carbon dioxide gas under pressure, either occurring naturally in mineral springs—historically prized in spa towns like Perrier in France—or produced artificially through mechanical carbonation, a process commercialized in the late 18th century. It has a neutral base flavor with a distinctive sharp, slightly acidic bite and effervescent tingle from the carbonic acid formed as CO2 dissolves, and a lively, fizzy texture that fades once opened. Used as a refreshing standalone drink, a mixer in cocktails, and a base for flavored sodas, carbonated water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, and offers the same trace minerals as its source water, with no meaningful nutritional difference from still water beyond the carbonation itself.

Ice is water in its solid state, forming when temperatures drop to or below 0°C (32°F), found naturally in glaciers, polar regions, and frost, and produced commercially or at home through refrigeration for use in food and beverages. It has no flavor or aroma of its own, taking on a hard, crystalline texture that can range from clear and dense to cloudy and brittle depending on freezing speed and mineral content. Used primarily for chilling drinks and food, preserving perishables, and in ice sculptures or winter sports, ice contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, offering the same trace minerals as its source water but purely a physical, non-nutritive ingredient.

Soy comes from the soybean, a legume domesticated in China around 3,000-5,000 years ago and long a dietary staple across East Asia, later spreading globally as both a food crop and major agricultural commodity. It has a mild, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a texture that varies enormously by form—from the firm bite of tofu and edamame to the smooth creaminess of soy milk and the meaty chew of tempeh. Extremely versatile, soy is used in countless forms including tofu, milk, sauce, and protein isolates, and stands out nutritionally as a complete plant protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with fiber, iron, and isoflavones linked to potential health benefits.

Okara is the fibrous pulp byproduct left over from pressing soybeans to make soy milk or tofu, a traditional ingredient in Japanese, Chinese, and Korean cooking where it's long been used to avoid food waste, particularly in dishes like Japanese unohana. It has a mild, slightly nutty, bean-like flavor with a dry, crumbly, fibrous texture similar to coarse meal. Used in stir-fries, veggie burgers, baked goods, and as a flour substitute, okara is notably rich in dietary fiber and retains a good amount of plant protein and calcium, though it's lower in protein than the soy milk or tofu it's derived from.

Vital wheat gluten is a concentrated protein extracted from wheat flour by washing away the starch, a process refined industrially in the 20th century to create a versatile baking additive. On its own it's bland and neutral in flavor, though it develops a chewy, meaty texture when hydrated and cooked. It's used to boost elasticity and rise in bread dough, and is a key ingredient in seitan and other plant-based meat substitutes. Nutritionally, it's exceptionally high in protein (over 75%) with very little fat or carbohydrate, though as pure gluten it's unsuitable for those with gluten intolerance or celiac disease.

Raising agents are substances added to baked goods to produce carbon dioxide gas and create rise and lightness, with early forms like yeast used since ancient Egyptian times, while chemical versions such as baking soda and baking powder were developed in the 19th century as faster, more reliable alternatives. They are essentially flavorless or very mildly bitter/metallic on their own, though excess use can leave a soapy or tinny aftertaste, and they work by releasing gas bubbles that get trapped in dough or batter, creating a light, airy texture. Used across breads, cakes, and pastries—commonly as baking soda, baking powder, yeast, or ammonium bicarbonate—raising agents are used in such small quantities that they contribute negligible calories or nutrients, functioning purely as a leavening tool rather than a nutritional ingredient.

Yeast is a single-celled fungus, most commonly Saccharomyces cerevisiae, used for thousands of years since ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian times to leaven bread and ferment beverages like beer and wine, long before its microbial nature was understood. It has a mild, slightly savory, umami flavor with a subtly yeasty, bread-like aroma, and comes in fresh, active dry, or instant forms that vary in texture from soft and crumbly to fine granules. Used in baking, brewing, and winemaking, yeast works by converting sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol through fermentation, and nutritional yeast (a deactivated form) is notably rich in B vitamins, protein, and often fortified with B12, making it a popular supplement for plant-based diets.

Nutritional yeast is a deactivated form of Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast, typically grown on molasses and then heat-killed before being dried into flakes or powder, popularized in the mid-20th century as a health food, particularly within vegan and vegetarian communities. It has a distinctly savory, cheesy, nutty flavor with umami depth, making it a popular seasoning sprinkled over popcorn, pasta, and salads or blended into vegan cheese sauces. Unlike active baking yeast, it has no leavening power since it's deactivated, but it stands out nutritionally as a complete protein source rich in B vitamins—often fortified with B12—making it especially valued in plant-based diets for filling that typical nutritional gap.

Baker's yeast is the common name for active Saccharomyces cerevisiae used specifically for baking, cultivated commercially since the late 19th century when compressed yeast production made it widely accessible, replacing older methods like sourdough starters and brewer's yeast. It has a mild, slightly savory flavor with little aroma on its own, though it develops the characteristic yeasty, bready aroma during fermentation, and is sold as fresh (compressed), active dry, or instant granules. Used to leaven bread, rolls, and pastries, baker's yeast works by converting sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, and while used in small quantities, it contributes trace amounts of B vitamins and protein alongside its primary leavening function.

SACCHAROMYCES CEREVISIAE is a species of yeast. It has been instrumental to winemaking, baking, and brewing since ancient times. S. cerevisiae is used in baking; the carbon dioxide generated by the fermentation is used as a leavening agent in bread and other baked goods. Historically, this use was closely linked to the brewing industry's use of yeast, as bakers took or bought the barm or yeast-filled foam from brewing ale from the brewers (producing the barm cake); today, brewing and baking yeast strains are somewhat different.

Yeast extract is a savory paste or powder made by breaking down yeast cells—typically through autolysis (self-digestion using the yeast's own enzymes) or hydrolysis—a byproduct process refined in the late 19th century that led to iconic products like Marmite in the UK and Vegemite in Australia. It has an intensely savory, salty, umami-rich flavor with deep, almost meaty notes, and comes as a thick, sticky spread or dried into a fine powder used as a seasoning. Used as a flavor enhancer in soups, sauces, stocks, and spreads, yeast extract is naturally rich in glutamic acid (contributing its umami punch), B vitamins, and protein, making it both a flavor booster and a modest nutritional contributor.

Sourdough is a naturally leavened bread made using a fermented starter of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria rather than commercial yeast, a method dating back thousands of years to ancient Egypt and still central to regional baking traditions like San Francisco's tangy loaves. It has a distinctive tangy, slightly sour flavor with a chewy, dense crumb and crisp, often blistered crust, shaped by the specific microbial culture of its starter, which can vary by region and even household. Made simply from flour, water, salt, and the starter culture, sourdough's slow fermentation is thought to improve digestibility and lower the glycemic impact compared to conventionally leavened bread, while offering fiber, B vitamins, and modest protein from the flour base.

Fruit is the mature, seed-bearing structure of flowering plants, cultivated and foraged by humans since prehistoric times across virtually every inhabited region, with different varieties native to tropical, temperate, and Mediterranean climates worldwide. It has an enormously varied flavor and texture profile—from the crisp sweetness of apples to the juicy tang of citrus and the soft, custardy richness of tropical fruits like mango—generally balancing natural sugars with acidity. Eaten fresh, dried, juiced, or cooked into jams, desserts, and savory dishes, fruit is prized nutritionally for its fiber, vitamins (especially vitamin C), antioxidants, and natural sugars, making it a nutrient-dense counterpart to refined sweeteners.

Berries are small, fleshy, typically sweet-tart fruits produced by a wide range of flowering plants, growing wild across temperate and cold regions worldwide long before cultivation, with varieties like strawberries, blueberries, raspberries, and blackberries becoming widely farmed staples in Europe and North America. They have a flavor ranging from intensely sweet to sharply tart, often balanced with floral or earthy notes, and a soft, juicy texture that varies from the delicate burst of raspberries to the firmer bite of blueberries. Eaten fresh, dried, or used in jams, baking, and beverages, berries are notably rich in antioxidants (especially anthocyanins), fiber, and vitamin C, making them among the most nutrient-dense fruits.

Juice is the liquid extracted from fruits or vegetables, produced by pressing, squeezing, or blending, with a history stretching back to ancient civilizations that fermented or drank fruit juices, though modern commercial juicing scaled up dramatically in the 20th century with pasteurization and packaging advances. It has a flavor that mirrors its source—sweet, tart, or a mix—with a smooth, liquid texture, sometimes with pulp retained for added body. Consumed as a beverage or used in cooking, baking, and cocktails, juice retains vitamins (especially vitamin C) and antioxidants from its source, though it typically lacks the fiber of whole fruit and can be concentrated in natural sugars, giving it a higher glycemic impact than eating the fruit whole.

Abiyuch comes from Crateva religiosa, commonly known as the sacred garlic pear or temple plant. It's a species of flowering tree that belongs to the caper family.

Apricots are stone fruits believed to have originated in China or Central Asia thousands of years ago, later spreading along the Silk Road through Persia and into the Mediterranean, where regions like Turkey and California became major modern producers. They have a delicate, sweet-tart flavor with subtle floral and honeyed notes, and a soft, velvety-skinned flesh that's juicy when ripe and firms into a chewy, concentrated sweetness when dried. Eaten fresh, dried, or used in jams, baking, and savory glazes, apricots are a good source of vitamin A (from beta-carotene), vitamin C, and fiber, with dried apricots also offering a notable concentration of iron and potassium.

Bananas are tropical fruits believed to have originated in Southeast Asia and Papua New Guinea thousands of years ago, later spreading through Africa and eventually the Americas, where they became one of the world's most widely consumed and traded fruits. They have a sweet, mild, slightly tangy flavor with a soft, creamy texture that ripens from starchy and firm to soft and sugary as the fruit matures. Eaten fresh, cooked, or dried, and used in baking, smoothies, and desserts, bananas are notably rich in potassium, vitamin B6, and fiber, along with natural sugars that make them a popular quick energy source.

Breadfruit is a starchy tropical fruit native to the South Pacific and Southeast Asia, long cultivated across Polynesian islands as a dietary staple, and historically significant for its role in the 18th-century Bounty voyage, which aimed to transplant it to the Caribbean as cheap food for enslaved laborers. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor reminiscent of fresh bread or potato when cooked, with a starchy, dense texture similar to a potato when roasted, boiled, or fried. Typically eaten cooked rather than raw, breadfruit is a good source of complex carbohydrates, fiber, potassium, and vitamin C, making it a nutrient-dense staple food in many tropical regions.

Carissa (commonly known as natal plum) is a small, glossy red fruit native to southern Africa, particularly South Africa, growing on a spiny shrub traditionally used both as a food source and an ornamental hedge in its native range. It has a tart, slightly sweet flavor often compared to a mix of cranberry and strawberry, with a soft, juicy flesh surrounding small seeds, though the unripe fruit and other plant parts contain a milky sap that's toxic if consumed. Eaten fresh, or used in jams, jellies, and sauces once ripe, carissa is a good source of vitamin C and antioxidants, though it remains a minor, largely regional fruit outside southern Africa.

Durian is a large, spiky tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia, particularly Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand, where it's been cultivated for centuries and earned the nickname "king of fruits" despite—or because of—its notoriously divisive smell. It has a custardy, rich, creamy texture with a complex flavor often described as a blend of sweet caramel, almond, and savory onion notes, paired with a famously pungent, sulfurous odor strong enough to be banned on public transport in parts of Southeast Asia. Eaten fresh or used in desserts, candies, and ice cream, durian is notably rich in healthy fats, fiber, vitamin C, and potassium, making it more calorie-dense and nutritious than most other fruits.

Cranberries come in two main varieties: the American cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon), native to North America and long used by Indigenous peoples before becoming a major commercial crop in states like Massachusetts and Wisconsin, and the smaller European cranberry (Vaccinium oxycoccos), native to boggy regions across Northern Europe and Asia and traditionally foraged rather than farmed. Both have a sharply tart, astringent flavor with a firm, crisp bite when fresh, though the European variety tends to be smaller and even more tart than its larger American cousin. Eaten fresh, dried, juiced, or made into sauces, cranberries are notably rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and compounds linked to urinary tract health, making them valued more for their functional benefits than their raw palatability.
Vaccinium macrocarpon (also called large cranberry, American cranberry and bearberry) is a North American species of cranberry of the subgenus Oxycoccus and genus Vaccinium.

Mammee apple (Mammea americana) is a large tropical fruit native to the Caribbean and northern South America, historically cultivated by Indigenous peoples across the region long before European colonization and still popular in Caribbean and Central American cuisines today. It has a sweet, aromatic flavor often compared to a blend of apricot, mango, and raspberry, with a firm, slightly fibrous orange flesh beneath a thick, rough brown-yellow rind that must be discarded along with the bitter seeds. Eaten fresh, or used in jams, juices, and desserts, mammee apple is a good source of vitamin C, fiber, and carotenoids, though it remains a relatively niche fruit outside its native tropical regions.

Mamey sapote (Pouteria sapota) is a large tropical fruit native to Central America and southern Mexico, cultivated by the Maya and Aztecs long before Spanish colonization and still widely grown across Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean today. It has a sweet, rich flavor often compared to a blend of sweet potato, pumpkin, and almond with honey-like notes, and a smooth, creamy, custard-like flesh beneath a rough, brown, sandpaper-textured skin. Eaten fresh, blended into milkshakes and desserts (notably popular in Cuban and Mexican cuisine), mamey sapote is a good source of vitamin C, vitamin A, and fiber, along with notable amounts of potassium.

A "brugnon" is a French word for a type of stone fruit closely related to the nectarine. In French, there's actually a distinction: Nectarine – the flesh separates easily from the pit (freestone); Brugnon – the flesh clings tightly to the pit (clingstone)

Native to China, brugnons spread along ancient trade routes into Persia and the Mediterranean, where Mediterranean climates now support major cultivation. The white-fleshed variety offers a delicate, low-acid sweetness compared to yellow varieties, with smooth, fuzz-free skin and flesh that clings to the pit. Consumed fresh as a snack or dessert fruit, it also features in salads, tarts, and preserves across various cuisines. Nutritionally, it provides vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber, along with natural sugars and antioxidant compounds, making it a commonly consumed seasonal stone fruit in temperate regions worldwide.

A rose apple (Syzygium jambos or related species) is a tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent. Despite its name, it's not related to either roses or apples — it belongs to the myrtle family. Pear- or bell-shaped fruit, usually pale yellow, white, pink, or red, with a waxy, smooth skin. Rowal (scientific name Pangium edule) is a tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands. The fruits are generally 15–30 cm long, with a rough brown exterior. The flesh has a strong aroma. The fresh fruit and seeds contain hydrogen cyanide and are DEADLY POISONOUS if consumed without prior preparation.

Sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) is a tropical fruit native to southern Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. It's a small to medium-sized fruit with rough, brown, potato-like skin. The flesh inside is yellowish-brown, soft, and grainy in texture. Often described as one of the sweetest fruits in the world. It has a rich, caramel-like or brown sugar flavor, sometimes with hints of vanilla and pear.

Soursop is a tropical fruit from the Annona muricata tree, native to the Caribbean, Central America, and parts of South America and Africa. Large, green, spiky/prickly on the outside — it can weigh anywhere from 1 to 7 kg. The inside is white, creamy, and fibrous with large black seeds. It's taste is an unique blend of sweet and tangy — often described as a mix of strawberry, pineapple, and citrus, with a creamy texture somewhat like banana or coconut.

A sugar apple (also called sweetsop) is a tropical fruit from the Annona squamosa tree, native to the tropical Americas and West Indies. It has a bumpy, knobby green skin made up of overlapping segments that look almost like scales or a pinecone. When ripe, the segments separate easily. The white, creamy flesh inside is sweet and custard-like — hence "sugar" apple. The taste is often described as a blend of vanilla, pear, and banana, with a grainy, melt-in-your-mouth texture.
A grape is a fruit, botanically a berry, of the deciduous woody vines of the flowering plant genus Vitis.

A RAISIN is a dried grape.
