SULTANA is a "white" (pale green), oval seedless grape variety also called the sultanina, Thompson Seedless, Lady de Coverly, and oval-fruited Kishmish.

Zante currants are small, dried, seedless grapes — despite the name, they're not actually related to fresh currants (which are berries from the Ribes genus). Dried fruits made from the Black Corinth grape.
Grape juice is obtained from crushing and blending grapes into a liquid.
This is a compound product made of concentrate grape juice and water.
Chasselas or Chasselas blanc is a wine grape variety grown in Switzerland, France, Germany, Portugal, Hungary, Romania, New Zealand and Chile.
Poulsard (also Ploussard) is a red French wine grape variety from the Jura wine region.
Pošip is an autochthonous white wine grape that is primarily grown in the Dalmatian region of Croatia on the island of Korčula, although small amounts are also being grown on the Pelješac Peninsula.
Sémillon is a golden-skinned grape used to make dry and sweet white wines, mostly in France and Australia.
Sylvaner or Silvaner is a variety of white wine grape grown primarily in Alsace and Germany, where its official name is Grüner Silvaner.
Syrah, also known as Shiraz, is a dark-skinned grape variety grown throughout the world and used primarily to produce red wine.
Teran grape is a variety of red grape from Istria, Croatia.
Trousseau or Trousseau Noir, also known as Bastardo, is an old variety of red wine grape originating in eastern France.

Strawberry guava (Psidium cattleianum) is a tropical fruit tree native to eastern Brazil. The flesh is white to creamy, with a sweet-tart taste reminiscent of a mix between strawberry and guava — hence the name. It contains small, hard seeds.
Fruit ou légume moyen, hors saison produit sous serre chauffée

Chicory greens are the leafy tops (and sometimes tender inner leaves) of the chicory plant (Cichorium intybus), a bitter leafy vegetable in the same family as endive and radicchio. They're used in cooking much like other bitter greens — think dandelion greens or escarole. Distinctly bitter, with a slight earthiness. The bitterness mellows a lot when cooked.

Cowpea leafy tips (sometimes called cowpea leaves, or by local names like "kunde" in Swahili, "ewedu" relatives, or "bean leaves") are the young, tender shoot tips and leaves of the cowpea plant (Vigna unguiculata) — the same plant that produces black-eyed peas. While most people know cowpeas for their beans, the leaves are widely eaten as a leafy green vegetable in parts of Africa (especially West and East Africa), as well as in South and Southeast Asia. Slightly bitter, earthy, spinach-like flavor, a bit more robust than spinach.
Chrysanthemum leaves seems to be the same, but an older/alternate label.

"Garland chrysanthemum" (also called tong ho in Chinese, shungiku in Japanese, and ssukgat in Korean) is an edible leafy green — not the ornamental flower you'd put in a bouquet, but a related plant (Glebionis coronaria) grown specifically for eating. Slightly bitter, herbal, and a little peppery — some describe it as tasting faintly like chrysanthemum tea smells.

Note that the translations between the various endives are not always clear. Nor do all languages distinguish between the  green part and the root. Endive in english is different from endive in french.
Cichorium endivia is a species of flowering plant belonging to the genus Cichorium, which is widely cultivated as one of the species of similar bitter-leafed vegetables known as endive and escarole.

Dock (genus Rumex, especially curly dock — Rumex crispus — and broad-leaved dock — Rumex obtusifolius) is a wild edible plant. Young leaves have a tart, lemony, slightly sour flavor thanks to oxalic acid — similar to sorrel but a bit milder. As leaves mature they get tougher and more bitter/astringent. Young leaves: eaten raw in salads, or added to soups, stews, and sautés like spinach.; Older leaves: usually cooked (boiled or braised) to mellow the sourness and soften the texture.

Small, oval-shaped leaflets of the moringa tree (Moringa oleifera), sometimes called the horseradish tree or ben tree. The leaves grow in clusters on the branches, often described as feathery or fern-like in arrangement. They're a popular vegetable in South Asian, Southeast Asian, and African cuisines. Added to salads, or cooked briefly like spinach — sautéed, added to soups, dals, or stir-fries.

Grape leaves (also called vine leaves) are the young, tender leaves of the grape plant (Vitis vinifera), used as a vegetable or wrap in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Balkan, and Caucasian cooking rather than eaten as a leafy green on their own. Slightly tart, earthy, a bit lemony — this comes mostly from the way they're brined or cooked (often with lemon juice).

Fiddlehead ferns are the tightly coiled, immature fronds of certain fern species, harvested in early spring before they unfurl. They're named for their resemblance to the curled end (scroll) of a fiddle or violin. Most common edible variety: Ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris) is the safest and most widely eaten species. Not all fern fiddleheads are edible — some are toxic, so identification matters. Often described as a cross between asparagus, green beans, and a slightly nutty, grassy taste. Fiddleheads must be cooked thoroughly (boiled or steamed for several minutes, then sautéed if desired) before eating. Raw or undercooked fiddleheads have caused foodborne illness outbreaks — they can carry bacteria or contain compounds that cause nausea, cramps, and diarrhea if not properly prepared.

Fireweed (Chamaenerion angustifolium, also called Epilobium angustifolium) is a tall wildflower with bright pink-purple flower spikes, common in northern temperate regions. Young leaves, picked before the plant flowers, can be eaten raw in salads or cooked like spinach. As the plant matures, the leaves get tougher and more bitter, so timing matters. Fireweed has a mild laxative effect in some people if eaten in quantity, so it's usually eaten in modest amounts rather than as a main dish.
RADICCHIO is a perennial cultivated form of leaf chicory (Cichorium intybus, Asteraceae) sometimes known as Italian chicory because of its common use in Italian cuisine.
Escarole, or broad-leaved endive (var latifolia), has broad, pale green leaves and is less bitter than the other varieties. Varieties or names include Batavian endive, grumolo, scarola, and scarole.
There is a mixup between the popular translations of Lactuca and Lactuca Sativa. Not sure which one should be used. For the moment they are combined.
Frillice iceberg lettuce is a cross of curly endive and iceberg lettuce, with the taste and texture of iceberg and the frilly top of the curly endive.

CHARD (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, Cicla-Group and Flavescens-Group) is a green leafy vegetable. Chard, like other green leafy vegetables, has highly nutritious leaves, making it a popular component of healthy diets.Fresh young chard can be used raw in salads. Mature chard leaves and stalks are typically cooked (like in pizzoccheri) or sautéed; the bitterness fades with cooking, leaving a refined flavor which is more delicate than that of cooked spinach.

The young, tender leaves of genus Corchorus (mainly Corchorus olitorius and Corchorus capsularis) are cooked and eaten as a green vegetable, similar to spinach or amaranth greens. When cooked, the leaves release a mucilaginous (slightly slimy) texture, somewhat like okra — this is prized in many cuisines for thickening soups and stews.
the latin name is also associated with mustard cabbage.

Mustard greens are the leafy tops of the mustard plant (Brassica juncea), and they're a true member of the mustard family — grown specifically for their peppery, pungent leaves rather than for seeds or oil (though the same plant family produces mustard seeds too). Mustard greens have a distinctly sharp, spicy, peppery bite — similar to the kick you get from horseradish, wasabi, or arugula, but more pronounced. Cooking mellows the heat somewhat, but they still have more punch than almost any other leafy green.

Mustard spinach, also known as komatsuna, is a leafy green vegetable that's actually part of the mustard/brassica family (Brassica rapa var. perviridis) rather than being related to true spinach. It's an East Asian vegetable, especially popular in Japanese cuisine (where it's called komatsuna), though it's also grown and eaten in China and other parts of Asia. The flavor is mild and slightly peppery.

New Zealand spinach (Tetragonia tetragonioides) isn't a true spinach at all. it's eaten much the same way as regular spinach — the young leaves and shoot tips are harvested and used cooked (steamed, sautéed, boiled, or added to soups and stir-fries). It's usually not eaten raw in large quantities because of its oxalate content, and cooking also helps soften its slightly thicker, fuzzier texture.

Vine spinach (also called Malabar spinach) is a tropical leafy green plant, not a true spinach but used similarly in cooking. It's especially popular in Indian, Filipino, and West African cooking, where it goes by various local names like poi saag (India) or slippery vegetable.

Water convolvulus (Ipomoea aquatica), also known as water spinach, morning glory, or kangkong, is a semi-aquatic tropical plant widely used as a leafy vegetable across Asia and Africa. It's a staple vegetable in cuisines across Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia). Both the leaves and tender stem tips are eaten, typically stir-fried with garlic, shrimp paste, or chili.

Across the Pacific and Caribbean, taro leaves show up in dishes like callaloo, and in parts of Asia and Africa they're simmered in coconut-based curries or soups. Raw taro leaves are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals, so they need thorough cooking.
PARSLEY or garden parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae
Broccoli is either the whole (flower+stalks), only the flowers or the leaves.
BROCCOLI is an edible green plant in the cabbage family whose large flowering head is eaten as a vegetable.

CAULIFLOWER is one of several vegetables in the species Brassica oleracea in the genus Brassica

Collards (collard greens) are a leafy green vegetable in the cabbage family — the same species as kale, cabbage, and broccoli (Brassica oleracea), just bred for large, loose, dark green leaves rather than a tight head. Earthy, slightly bitter, and hearty — milder than mustard greens, tougher and more assertive than spinach. Traditionally slow-cooked (often with smoked meat, onion, garlic, vinegar, and pepper flakes in Southern U.S. cooking) until tender — but they can also be sautéed, steamed, or even eaten raw/massaged in salads if sliced thin. It's the same species as cabbage (Brassica oleracea), but not a cabbage in the way we normally mean the word.

Chinese broccoli (also called gai lan or kai lan, 芥蓝) is actually a distinct vegetable from regular broccoli, though they're related. Both belong to the Brassica oleracea species and the broader cabbage family. Gai lan has long, thick green stalks with flat, broad leaves and small, scattered flower buds. Western broccoli has a large, compact floret head on a thick stalk. It's slightly more bitter and robust than regular broccoli, with an earthy, slightly peppery flavor.
CELERY (Apium graveolens) is a marshland plant in the family Apiaceae that has been cultivated as a vegetable since antiquity.

FENNEL (Foeniculum vulgare) is a flowering plant species in the carrot family. The bulb, foliage, and fruits of the fennel plant are used in many of the culinary traditions of the world. The bulb is a crisp vegetable that can be sautéed, stewed, braised, grilled, or eaten raw. Young tender leaves are used for garnishes, as a salad, to add flavor to salads, to flavor sauces to be served with puddings, and also in soups and fish sauce.

RHUBARB is a cultivated plant in the genus Rheum in the family Polygonaceae. Rhubarb is stewed with sugar or used in pies and desserts, but it can also be put into savoury dishes or pickled. Rhubarb can be dehydrated and infused with fruit juice.

Arrowhead (also called Sagittaria, water arrowhead, or 慈姑 cí gū in Chinese) is an aquatic plant whose starchy corms (bulb-like root tubers) are eaten as a vegetable. It grows in shallow ponds, marshes, and rice paddies, and is especially popular in Chinese, Japanese, and Southeast Asian cooking. Mildly bitter and slightly sweet, with a starchy texture similar to a chestnut or potato. The bitterness mellows considerably with cooking.

Arrowroot (Maranta arundinacea) is a tropical plant native to the Caribbean and Central/South America. It's a rhizome — an underground stem, similar in concept to ginger or turmeric. Arrowroot is most famous as a starch/thickener rather than a table vegetable.

Die Artischocke (Cynara cardunculus subsp. scolymus (L.) Hegi, Syn.: Cynara scolymus L.) ist eine distelartige, kräftige Kulturpflanze aus der Familie der Korbblütler. Die Sortengruppe der Artischocken wird wegen ihrer essbaren knospigen Blütenstände angebaut und als Blütengemüse verzehrt.

The globe ARTICHOKE (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus), also known as French artichoke and green artichoke in the USA, is a variety of a species of thistle cultivated as a food. Leaves are often removed one at a time, and the fleshy base eaten, with hollandaise, vinegar, butter, mayonnaise, aioli, lemon juice, or other sauces. The fibrous upper part of each leaf is usually discarded. The heart is eaten when the inedible choke has been peeled away from the base and discarded. The thin leaves covering the choke are also edible.

L’artichaut (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus (L.) Benth.) est une plante de la famille des Astéracées. On désigne sous le nom d'artichaut à la fois la plante entière et sa partie comestible. Les têtes d'artichaut sont consommées soit crues soit cuites.
Il carciofo (Cynara cardunculus subsp. scolymus) è una pianta angiosperma dicotiledone della famiglia Asteraceae coltivata in Italia e in altri Paesi per uso alimentare.
De artisjok (Cynara scolymus) is een plant uit de composietenfamilie. De vlezige schutbladeren van het gesloten bloemhoofdje worden als groente gegeten.
Uma alcachofra (Cynara cardunculus subsp. scolymus) é uma planta com até um metro de altura, da família das compostas.

Asparagus, or garden asparagus, folk name sparrow grass, scientific name Asparagus officinalis is a spring vegetable, a flowering perennial plant species in the genus Asparagus;

Kanpyo is a Japanese ingredient made from dried strips of gourd — specifically the flesh of the calabash or bottle gourd (a variety called yūgao, related to what's sometimes called "bottle gourd" or "calabash" in English). To make it, the gourd is peeled into long, thin ribbons, then sun-dried until they become firm, chewy strips. Before use, the dried strips are rehydrated and usually simmered in a mixture of soy sauce, sugar, and mirin (or dashi) until they turn a light brown color and take on a sweet-savory flavor.

A balsam pear is another name for bitter melon (Momordica charantia), a tropical vine in the gourd family. It's widely grown across Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, and South America. True to both its names, it has a pronounced bitter taste — the most bitter of any commonly eaten vegetable.
The bamboos are evergreen perennial flowering plants in the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae.
Bamboo shoots or bamboo sprouts are the edible shoots (new bamboo culms that come out of the ground) of many bamboo species including Bambusa vulgaris and Phyllostachys edulis.

The young sprouts/suckers that grow off the main corm (sometimes called "huli" in Hawaiian), which are more often used for propagating new plants than eating, though tender young shoots can be cooked too.

Broccoli raab (also spelled rabe, and sometimes called rapini) is a leafy green vegetable popular in Italian and Mediterranean cooking. Despite its name, it's not closely related to regular broccoli — it's actually more closely related to turnips. It has long, thin stalks with dark green, slightly jagged leaves and small florets that resemble tiny broccoli heads. The whole plant is edible — leaves, stems, and florets. Its defining characteristic is a pleasantly bitter, slightly pungent, nutty flavor, much more assertive than regular broccoli.

Burdock root is an edible root vegetable and herbal remedy that comes from the burdock plant (Arctium lappa), a large-leafed plant native to northern Asia and Europe, now grown worldwide. it's especially popular in Japanese cuisine, where it's known as gobō. It has a mildly sweet, earthy flavor and a crunchy texture.

Celtuce (also called stem lettuce, celery lettuce, or Chinese lettuce) is a vegetable that's actually a cultivar of the same species as regular lettuce (Lactuca sativa), but it's grown specifically for its thick, edible stem rather than its leaves. The stem has a mild, slightly sweet, and nutty flavor with a crisp, crunchy texture — often compared to a cross between celery, cucumber, and asparagus.

Fuki (Petasites japonicus) is a flowering plant native to Europe and parts of Asia and North America. In Japanese cuisine, fuki is a well-established vegetable and has been eaten for centuries: The leaf stalks (petioles) are the main edible part — boiled, then peeled and used in simmered dishes (nimono), stir-fries, or as a side dish; The flower buds (fuki no tō) are a beloved spring delicacy, eaten tempura-fried or as a miso paste — they have a pleasant, slightly bitter taste.

Mustard Cabbage (also called gai choy or Chinese mustard) is a leafy green vegetable common in Asian cuisine. Large, crinkled or smooth leaves, often with a pale green or yellowish color; can look somewhat like bok choy or napa cabbage. Distinctly pungent and slightly bitter, with a mustardy kick that mellows when cooked.
The heart of palm is the inner core of certain palm trees, harvested as a vegetable and typically canned or jarred in brine.

Pokeberry (pokeweed, Phytolacca americana) shoots are a traditional Southern U.S. food, often called "poke sallet" or "poke salad." The plant is toxic, but very young shoots can be made edible through careful preparation.

Allium fistulosum, the Welsh onion, also commonly called bunching onion, long green onion, Japanese bunching onion, and spring onion, is a species of perennial plant. A. fistulosum is an ingredient in Asian cuisine, especially in East and Southeast Asia. In the West, A. fistulosum is primarily used as a scallion or salad onion.

NDB number 11294 used as a general "sweet onion" category — it's also commonly cited as the stand-in nutrition data for Vidalia onions specifically, since Vidalia is considered a brand/regional name rather than a distinct variety with its own USDA entry.
The SHALLOT is a type of onion, specifically a botanical variety of the species Allium cepa.

A tuber is a swollen underground stem (or in some cases a swollen root), used for storing nutrients — like potatoes. It typically grows at the end of a rhizome or stolon, not as the plant's central root.

Eppaw is the edible tuber of the duck potato plant (Sagittaria latifolia, also called wapato or arrowhead), traditionally eaten by some Native American groups, particularly noted in Seminole/Florida contexts. It's a starchy, potato-like root vegetable that grows in shallow water and marshes, and was historically gathered as a wild food source.

Root has pale tan or beige skin, with white flesh. Native to the Mediterranean; naturalized widely, including in North America, with the classic "oyster-like" flavor that gave it its common name.

A sweet potato is a starchy root vegetable. It grows underground as a swollen root, It's skin can be orange, purple, white, or reddish; flesh is often orange, but also comes in white or purple. It has a naturally sweet flavor, especially when roasted or baked. It is rich in beta-carotene (converts to vitamin A) and a good source of fiber, vitamin C, potassium, and manganese, and has complex carbohydrates, so it digests more slowly than many other starches

TAPIOCA is a starch extracted from cassava root (tapioca seems to be the same as tapioca starch, but not used as such on ingredient lists)

Tapioca pearls are made from cassava root starch, a plant native to South America but now cultivated widely across Brazil, Southeast Asia, and Africa. On their own, dry pearls are essentially flavorless and starchy, taking on a mild sweetness and chewy, translucent texture once cooked. They're most commonly used in bubble tea, puddings, and Southeast Asian desserts, or as a thickener in soups and pie fillings. Nutritionally, tapioca is mostly pure carbohydrate with very little protein, fiber, or micronutrients, making it a gluten-free energy source but not a significant source of other nutrients.

Yam is the common name for some plant species in the genus Dioscorea (family Dioscoreaceae) that form edible tubers. In some places, other (unrelated) root vegetables are sometimes referred to as "yams".

Japanese mountain yam is native to China and Japan. Unlike most yams, it's often eaten raw — grated, it becomes sticky and mucilaginous (called tororo in Japanese cooking), used as a topping for rice, soba, or mixed into batters. It can also be cooked (steamed, boiled, fried).
The POTATO is a starchy, tuberous crop from the perennial nightshade Solanum tuberosum.
In Hawaii specifically, "Tahitian" is also a distinct named cultivar — it was introduced from Tahiti by horticulturist Gerrit Parmile Wilder.

Yambean is a tropical legume (in the bean family, Fabaceae) grown primarily for its large, starchy, edible tuber/root. Native to Mexico and Central America, widely cultivated across Latin America and Southeast Asia. Mildly sweet, very crunchy, similar to a cross between an apple and a water chestnut — it stays crisp even when cooked.

Yautia (also called malanga or taro coco) is a starchy root vegetable widely used in Latin American and Caribbean cuisine. Earthy, slightly nutty flavor, denser and less slimy than taro. When cooked, it becomes soft and starchy — similar to a potato but with more depth of flavor.

Crudités (plural only) are traditional French appetizers consisting of sliced or whole raw vegetables[1] which are typically dipped in a vinaigrette or other dipping sauce. Examples of crudités include celery sticks, carrot sticks, cucumber sticks, bell pepper strips, broccoli, cauliflower, fennel, and asparagus spears.

Die Avocado (Persea americana) ist eine Pflanzenart aus der Familie der Lorbeergewächse (Lauraceae). Die Avocadofrucht ist eine einsamige Beere. Im deutschen Handel findet sich hauptsächlich der weltweit meistverbreitete Typ Fuerte.

The AVOCADO (Persea americana) is a tree classified as a member of the flowering plant family Lauraceae. The fruit of the plant, also called an avocado, is botanically a large berry containing a single large seed.

Persea americana, llamado popularmente aguacate, palto o aguacatero, es una especie arbórea del género Persea perteneciente a la familia Lauraceae, cuyo fruto, el aguacate o palta, es una baya comestible.

L'avocatier (Persea americana) est une espèce d'arbres fruitiers de la famille des Lauracées, originaire du Mexique et d'Amérique centrale. Il est notamment cultivé pour ses fruits, les avocats, riches en lipides.
L'avocado (Persea americana) è una specie arborea da frutto che appartiene alla famiglia delle Lauracee.
De avocado (Persea americana) is een boom uit Centraal-Amerika. Hij is bekend om zijn gelijknamige voor consumptie geschikte vrucht.

Borretsch (Borago officinalis), ist eine zur Familie der Raublattgewächse (Boraginaceae) gehörige Pflanze. Sie wird als Gewürz- und Heilpflanze verwendet. Die Blätter des Borretschs werden in Salaten gegessen oder in Suppen gekocht.
Borage, also known as a starflower, is an annual herb in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae. It is native to the Mediterranean region. Borage is used as either a fresh vegetable or a dried herb.

Borago officinalis, la borraja, es una especie fanerógama perteneciente a la familia de las boragináceas. La forma de cocinarla es variada, pues se emplea de diferentes maneras toda la planta, desde los tallos, hasta las hojas.

La Bourrache ou Bourrache officinale (Borago officinalis) est une espèce de plantes annuelles de la famille des Boraginacées. Les fleurs de bourrache et les jeunes feuilles se consomment traditionnellement à l'état frais.
La borragine (Borago officinalis L.) è una pianta erbacea annuale della famiglia delle Boraginaceae. Le foglie giovani sono variamente impiegate in cucina.

De bernagie (Borago officinalis), ook vaak komkommerkruid genoemd, is een gemakkelijk herkenbare, ruwharige, eenjarige plant met blauwe bloemen. Als voedsel wordt de plant vooral in het Middellandse Zeegebied gewaardeerd als onderdeel van salades en andere zomerse gerechten.
Borragem (Borago officinalis L.), é uma planta herbácea anual mediterrânea. Folhas e flores são utilizadas.
ALOE VERA is a succulent plant species of the genus Aloe.

"Drumstick" is the common name for the long, slender seed pods of the moringa tree (Moringa oleifera), sometimes called the horseradish tree or ben tree. They're a popular vegetable in South Asian, Southeast Asian, and African cuisines. Long, thin, ridged green pods, often 1–3 feet long. Mild, slightly sweet, a bit like asparagus or green beans.
Konjac is a common name of the East and Southeast Asian plant Amorphophallus konjac (syn. A. rivieri), which has an edible corm (bulbo-tuber).

HORSERADISH (Armoracia rusticana, syn. Cochlearia armoracia) is a perennial plant of the family Brassicaceae. The intact horseradish root has hardly any aroma. When cut or grated enzymes from the now-broken plant cells break down sinigrin (a glucosinolate) to produce allyl isothiocyanate (mustard oil), which irritates the mucous membranes of the sinuses and eyes. Grated mash should be used immediately or preserved in vinegar for best flavor.

JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE (Helianthus tuberosus), also called sunroot, sunchoke, earth apple, or topinambour, is a species of sunflower. The tubers are sometimes used as a substitute for potatoes: they have a similar consistency, and in their raw form have a similar texture, but a sweeter, nuttier flavor; raw and sliced thinly, they are fit for a salad.
The PARSNIP (Pastinaca sativa) is a root vegetable closely related to the carrot and parsley.
White Icicle radish is a heirloom radish variety, notable for its long, slender white root. Milder and less peppery-hot than round red radishes, with a crisp, juicy bite.

Nopales are the edible pads (paddles) of the prickly pear cactus (genus Opuntia), widely used in Mexican cuisine. Slightly tart and grassy, a bit like green beans or okra, with a similar mucilaginous (slightly slimy) texture when cooked, especially if simmered.

"White-flowered gourd" (calabash) refers to Lagenaria siceraria — also known as bottle gourd, calabash gourd, opo squash, or long melon. It's the same plant whose hard-shelled fruits are dried and used as bottles, bowls, or musical instruments, but when eaten as food it's harvested young and tender, before the shell hardens. Very mild, slightly sweet, with a texture similar to zucchini or chayote — it takes on the flavor of whatever it's cooked with. Common in cuisines: South Asian (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh — called lauki, doodhi, or ghiya), Chinese (hu lu), Vietnamese, Italian (cucuzza), and West African cooking. One caution worth knowing: bottle gourds can occasionally develop high levels of cucurbitacins (the compound that makes some gourds bitter), which can cause food poisoning. The rule of thumb is — if it tastes bitter, don't eat it, even if just one bite.

"Dishcloth gourd" (also called towel gourd, sponge gourd, or luffa) is the common name for Luffa — usually Luffa aegyptiaca (smooth luffa) or Luffa acutangula (angled/ridged luffa, sometimes called "Chinese okra"). It's a tropical vine in the cucumber/squash family, common in Asian, African, and some Mediterranean cuisines. The flesh is mild, slightly sweet, and a bit like a cross between zucchini and cucumber, with a spongy texture that softens when cooked.

Winged beans (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus) are a tropical legume known for their distinctive four-sided, ruffled or "winged" pods — the edges look like jagged ribbons running down the length of each pod. Almost the entire plant is edible: pods, seeds, leaves, flowers, and even the tuberous roots can all be eaten. That's unusual among legumes. High in protein: the seeds in particular are very protein- and nutrient-dense, which is part of why they've been studied as a potential "supercrop" for tropical regions. Native to Southeast Asia and New Guinea, and widely grown across South and Southeast Asia, as well as parts of Africa.

Yardlong beans (also called Chinese long beans, snake beans, or asparagus beans) are a type of legume known for their dramatically long, slender pods — typically 12 to 30 inches long, though they're usually picked and sold around 18 inches. They have a slightly nuttier, more savory flavor than regular green beans, with a denser, chewier texture that holds up well to high-heat cooking like stir-frying. They're a staple in Chinese, Southeast Asian (especially Thai, Vietnamese, Filipino), and South Asian cooking.

The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) recognizes 11 categories of pulses: Dry beans — includes kidney beans, navy beans, pinto beans, black beans, lima beans, mung beans, adzuki beans; Dry broad beans — fava beans, horse beans, broad beans (in dried form); Dry peas — includes split peas, whole dried peas (green or yellow); Chickpeas — also called garbanzo beans; Dry cowpeas — black-eyed peas, blackeye beans; Pigeon peas — also called Congo beans or gandules; Lentils — includes red, green, brown, black (beluga), French (Puy); Bambara beans — also called Bambara groundnuts (earth peas); Vetches — common vetch; Lupins — lupin beans (also called lupini beans); Minor pulses — a catch-all for less common ones, such as lablab, jack beans, winged beans, yam beans

Hyacinth beans (Lablab purpureus, also called lablab beans, dolichos beans, or Egyptian beans) are a fast-growing climbing vine grown both as an ornamental plant and a food crop. The young, immature pods can be cooked and eaten like green beans. However, the mature beans and pods contain cyanogenic glycosides and must be thoroughly cooked (usually boiled with water changes) before eating — they're toxic raw or undercooked. In parts of Africa and Asia, they're a significant food crop and protein source when properly prepared.

Black field beans (Vicia faba) are a small, dark-seeded variety of the broad/fava bean family, traditionally grown across Europe and the UK as a hardy field crop suited to cooler climates. They have a rich, earthy, slightly sweet flavor with a dense, starchy texture. Commonly used in soups, stews, and traditional dishes, they're also valued in sustainable farming as a nitrogen-fixing rotation crop and livestock feed. Nutritionally, they're an excellent source of plant protein and fiber, along with iron, folate, and B vitamins, making them a hearty, economical addition to plant-based diets.

Native to South Asia, horse gram is an ancient, drought-resistant legume long cultivated across India, Nepal, and parts of Africa and Southeast Asia, where it's also used as livestock fodder. Small, flattish, and reddish-brown, it has a robust, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a firm bite. Traditionally simmered into soups, stews, and sprouted dishes, or ground into flour, it's especially prized in South Indian cuisine (like kulith usal). Nutritionally, it stands out among pulses for its exceptional protein, iron, and calcium content, along with dietary fiber, making it a valued, if underappreciated, global superfood.

Green gram, whole (Vigna radiata), commonly known as mung bean or moong, originated in the Indian subcontinent and spread across Asia and beyond through centuries of trade and cultivation. Sold whole with its green skin intact, it has a mild, slightly sweet, earthy flavor and a firm texture that softens on cooking. It's used worldwide in soups, stews, curries, salads, and sprouts, and is especially popular in Asian cuisines from India to China and Southeast Asia. Nutritionally, it's rich in plant protein, dietary fiber, folate, potassium, and magnesium, making it a light, easily digestible legume valued globally for everyday and health-focused diets.

Cowpeas (Vigna unguiculata), also known as black-eyed peas or southern peas, originated in West Africa thousands of years ago before spreading to the Mediterranean, Asia, and the Americas via trade and slavery routes. They have an earthy, mildly nutty flavor with a creamy texture once cooked. Versatile in the kitchen, they're used in stews, salads, fritters (like akara), rice dishes (such as Hoppin' John), and purees. Nutritionally, cowpeas are a powerhouse: high in plant-based protein and fiber, rich in folate, iron, magnesium, and potassium, and naturally low in fat—making them a staple for heart-healthy, budget-friendly diets worldwide.

Peas are a good example of how the same plant can fall into different categories depending on how it's harvested and used. Fresh peas (green peas, snap peas, snow peas) are harvested young and eaten fresh, in or out of the pod. they are classified as a vegetable, not a pulse. Dried peas are the same plant, but the peas are left to mature and dry on the vine before harvesting. This is what counts as a pulse.

Chickpeas (Cicer arietinum), also known as garbanzo beans, are one of the world's oldest cultivated legumes, originating in the Middle East over 7,000 years ago and now grown widely across the Mediterranean, India, and the Americas. They have a mild, slightly nutty, earthy flavor with a firm yet creamy texture once cooked, making them extremely versatile in the kitchen. Chickpeas star in dishes like hummus, falafel, curries, soups, salads, and roasted snacks, and can be ground into flour for flatbreads and fritters. Nutritionally, they're a powerhouse: rich in plant-based protein, fiber, complex carbohydrates, iron, folate, and manganese, while being naturally low in fat. Their high fiber and protein content supports digestion, blood sugar stability, and satiety, making chickpeas a staple for vegetarian, vegan, and heart-healthy diets worldwide.

Originating in the Fertile Crescent over 8,000 years ago, lentils spread across the Mediterranean, Middle East, South Asia, and beyond, becoming a dietary cornerstone worldwide. Known as "dal" in South Asia, they come in many varieties—red, green, brown, black, yellow—each with subtly different flavor, from mild and sweet to earthy. Quick-cooking and hulling-friendly, lentils are simmered into soups, stews, curries, and purées across cuisines, from Indian dal tadka to French lentille du Puy salads and Middle Eastern mujadara. Nutritionally, they're a powerhouse of plant protein, fiber, iron, and folate, making them a global staple for sustainable, affordable nutrition.

Beechnuts are the small, triangular nuts produced by beech trees (genus Fagus), particularly the American beech (Fagus grandifolia) and European beech (Fagus sylvatica). A hickory nut is the edible nut produced by trees in the genus Carya — the same genus that includes pecans. They're native mostly to North America, with a few species in Asia. Flavor varies a lot by species — some, like shagbark hickory, are sweet and rich (similar to a pecan, which makes sense given the family connection), while others, like pignut hickory, can be bitter or astringent.

Native to Mexico and Guatemala, chia seeds come from the flowering plant Salvia hispanica. Black seeds are the traditional, more widely available variety; white seeds are a naturally occurring lighter variant, often prized for their appearance in pale-colored dishes. Both share a mild, nutty flavor and neutral taste, absorbing surrounding flavors easily. When soaked, they develop a gel-like texture, making them ideal for puddings, smoothies, baked goods, and as an egg substitute. Nutritionally identical, both are rich in fiber, plant-based omega-3s, protein, calcium, and antioxidants — a versatile, nutrient-dense addition to any diet.

Cottonseed is the seed of the cotton plant (genus Gossypium), harvested as a byproduct of cotton fiber production. After cotton bolls are picked, the fluffy fiber (lint) is separated from the seeds during a process called ginning. Each cotton boll contains several seeds embedded in the fiber. Raw cottonseed contains a natural compound called gossypol, which is toxic to humans in significant quantities. Some specialty "glandless" cotton varieties have been bred to have naturally low gossypol levels, and these are sometimes explored as a protein source (the seed kernel is fairly protein-rich), but this isn't mainstream or widely available commercially.

CARAWAY (Carum carvi), is a biennial plant in the family Apiaceae. The fruits, usually used whole, have a pungent, anise-like flavor. Caraway is used as a spice in breads, especially rye bread. Caraway is also used in desserts, liquors, casseroles, and other foods.

The CAYENNE PEPPER is a type of Capsicum annuum. It is usually a moderately hot chili pepper used to flavor dishes.

CURRY POWDER is a spice mix originating from the Indian subcontinent.

TURMERIC is a flowering plant of the ginger family, Zingiberaceae, the roots of which are used in cooking. Note that turmeric contains some curcumine (E100).

CINNAMOMUM VERUM, called true cinnamon tree or Ceylon cinnamon tree is a small evergreen tree belonging to the family Lauraceae, native to Sri Lanka.
CLOVEs are the aromatic flower buds of a tree in the family Myrtaceae, Syzygium aromaticum.
GINGER (Zingiber officinale) is a flowering plant whose rhizome, ginger root or simply ginger, is widely used as a spice or a folk medicine

A PINK PEPPERCORN is a dried berry of the shrub Schinus molle, commonly known as the Peruvian peppertree. Although a peppercorn is the dried fruit of a plant from the genus Piper, pink peppercorns came to be called such because they resemble peppercorns, and because they, too, have a peppery flavour. As they are members of the cashew family, they may cause allergic reactions including anaphylaxis for persons with a tree nut allergy.

dill (anethum graveolens) is an annual herb in the celery family apiaceae. dill is widely grown in eurasia where its leaves and seeds are used as a herb or spice for flavouring food.

Epazote (Dysphania ambrosioides, formerly Chenopodium ambrosioides) is a pungent, aromatic herb widely used in Mexican and Central American cooking. The flavor is hard to pin down — people describe it as a mix of citrus, mint, anise, tar, and even petroleum-like notes. It's strong, so it's used in moderation, usually just a sprig or a few leaves per dish, added toward the end of cooking to preserve its aroma. Epazote contains compounds (like ascaridole) that can be toxic in concentrated amounts, such as in essential oil form. Using fresh or dried leaves in normal cooking quantities is considered safe and is how it's traditionally consumed — but it shouldn't be consumed as a concentrated extract or in medicinal "high dose" preparations.

TARRAGON (Artemisia dracunculus), is a species of perennial herb in the sunflower family. Tarragon is one of the four fines herbes of French cooking, and is particularly suitable for chicken, fish, and egg dishes.
THYME is an aromatic perennial evergreen herb with culinary, medicinal, and ornamental uses. The most common variety is Thymus vulgaris.
Marjoram (Origanum majorana) is a somewhat cold-sensitive perennial herb or undershrub with sweet pine and citrus flavors.
Oregano (Origanum vulgare) is a flowering plant in the mint family (Lamiaceae).
Coriander (Coriandrum sativum), also known as cilantro or Chinese parsley, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.
Juniper as an ingredient most certainly implies a juniper berry.

JUNIPERS are coniferous plants in the genus Juniperus of the cypress family Cupressaceae. Juniper berries are a spice used in a wide variety of culinary dishes and best known for the primary flavoring in gin. Juniper berry sauce is often a popular flavoring choice for quail, pheasant, veal, rabbit, venison and other game dishes.

A JUNIPER BERRY is the female seed cone produced by the various species of junipers. Juniper berries are used in northern European and particularly Scandinavian cuisine to "impart a sharp, clear flavor" to meat dishes. Besides Norwegian and Swedish dishes, juniper berries are also sometimes used in German, Austrian, Czech, Polish and Hungarian cuisine, often with roasts (such as German sauerbraten). Northern Italian cuisine, especially that of the South Tyrol, also incorporates juniper berries.

The flowers come from Sesbania grandiflora, a fast-growing tropical tree also called the vegetable hummingbird, hummingbird tree, or agati. It's a popular edible flower across South and Southeast Asian cuisines. Before cooking, the bitter stamens and pistil inside each flower are usually pinched out, leaving the sweeter petals. They taste mildly sweet and slightly bitter, with a delicate, slightly crunchy texture once cooked.
WASABI (Eutrema japonicum or Wasabia japonica) or Japanese horseradish is a plant of the Brassicaceae family.

CHLORELLA is a genus of single-celled green algae belonging to the division Chlorophyta.

Spirulina is a blue-green algae (cyanobacterium) that's grown and processed as a food and dietary supplement. Very high in protein (roughly 55–70% by dry weight), including all essential amino acids. Rich in B vitamins (especially B12-like compounds, though its B12 isn't well-absorbed by humans), iron, and antioxidants like phycocyanin (the pigment giving it its blue-green color). It contains omega-6 fatty acids (notably gamma-linolenic acid)

Palmaria palmata, also called dulse, dillisk or dilsk (from Irish/Scottish Gaelic duileasc/duileasg), red dulse, sea lettuce flakes, or creathnach, is a red alga (Rhodophyta) previously referred to as Rhodymenia palmata.
Fucus is a genus of brown algae found in the intertidal zones of rocky seashores almost throughout the world.

Queller (Salicornia) ist eine Pflanzengattung in der Familie der Fuchsschwanzgewächse (Amaranthaceae). Insbesondere Europäischer Queller und Salicornia bigelovii sind essbar und wohlschmeckend, wenn auch recht salzig. Sie sind eher im gastronomischen Bereich oder im Großhandel erhältlich.

Salicornia is a genus of succulent, halophyte (salt tolerant) flowering plants in the family Amaranthaceae that grow in salt marshes, on beaches, and among mangroves. The main European species is often eaten and the main North American species is occasionally sold in grocery stores or appears on restaurant menus, usually as 'sea beans' or samphire greens or sea asparagus.

Le genre Salicornia regroupe une trentaine d'espèces de plantes halophytes appartenant à la famille des Amaranthaceae. En France, la majorité de la salicorne produite est ramassée en bords de mer et plus particulièrement dans les zones de marais salés.

Zeekraal (Salicornia) is een geslacht van zoutverdragende succulenten uit de amarantenfamilie. Zeekraal kan tegen onderdompeling in zout water. Gekookt of rauw is het eetbaar. Na het koken lijkt het qua kleur op zeewier. De smaak en structuur lijken op jonge spinaziestengels.

Tsunomata (角叉, or つのまた) is the Japanese name for a type of red algae/seaweed. In Japanese cooking, it's traditionally soaked and used in salads, soups, or as a crunchy/chewy garnish. It has a mild, subtle sea flavor rather than a strong "seaweed" taste.

Laver is a type of edible seaweed — specifically a red algae from the genus Porphyra (and related species like Pyropia). It grows on rocks in intertidal zones along coastlines, particularly in the UK, Ireland, Japan, Korea, and other coastal regions. It has a savory, briny, slightly mineral taste — often described as umami-rich, similar to other seaweeds.
Laver nd nori are essentially the same organism prepared differently — the distinction is mostly about processing and tradition rather than the plant itself.
Nori (海苔) is the Japanese name for edible seaweed (a "sea vegetable") species of the red algae genus Pyropia, including P. yezoensis and P. tenera.

HIMANTHALIA ELONGATA is a brown alga (class Phaeophyta or Phaeophyceae) in the order Fucales, also known by the common names thongweed, sea thong and sea spaghetti.

Kelp is a type of large brown seaweed that grows in cold, nutrient-rich coastal waters, and it's become a fairly common food ingredient, especially in East Asian cuisines. Kelp is notably rich in iodine, along with other minerals like calcium, magnesium, and iron. It's low in calories and contains some fiber. It has a natural savory, oceanic taste often described as umami. Kelp is a common term covering many species across several genera, all in the order Laminariales.

KOMBU (from Japanese: 昆布, translit. konbu) is edible kelp from mostly the family Laminariaceae and is widely eaten in East Asia. There are about eighteen edible species in Laminariaceae and most of them, but not all, are called kombu.
Kombu breton (Laminaria digitata), séchée ou déshydratée

Saccharina japonica is a marine species of the Phaeophyceae (brown algae) plant , a type of kelp or seaweed, that is extensively cultivated on ropes between the seas of Japan and Korea.[
Wakame (ワカメ), UNDARIA PINNATIFIDA, is a species of edible seaweed, a type of marine algae, and a sea vegetable.

Irish moss (Chondrus crispus), also called sea moss, is a red seaweed that grows along rocky Atlantic coastlines, especially around Ireland and the Caribbean. In food, it's valued mainly for the natural gelling and thickening properties it gets from carrageenan, a compound extracted from its cell walls. It has a mild, slightly salty or neutral taste on its own, so it's usually blended into other foods rather than eaten plain.

AGARICUS BISPORUS is an edible basidiomycete mushroom native to grasslands in Europe and North America.

Agaricus bisporus is a single species that's sold under several names depending on maturity and color strain: white button mushrooms (young, white variety), crimini/baby bella (young, brown variety), and portobello (mature, brown variety, large cap). So "white mushrooms" specifically denotes the white cultivar picked at an early stage.

Button mushroom and white mushroom both refer to young Agaricus bisporus, harvested early before the cap opens up. "Button" describes the shape/size (small, round, unopened cap), while "white" describes the color strain.

LACTARIUS is a genus of mushroom-producing, ectomycorrhizal fungi, containing several edible species.

Enoki mushrooms (also called enokitake, golden needle mushrooms, or velvet shank) are a type of edible mushroom (Flammulina velutipes or filiformis) commonly used in East Asian cuisine, especially Japanese, Korean, and Chinese cooking. Mild, slightly sweet, and faintly fruity flavor; crisp, crunchy texture, even after cooking; Often described as having a delicate, almost noodle-like quality

Fresh pepeiao has a convex shape with a smooth, sometimes wrinkly surface, and can be a purply gray-brown color. It has a slightly chewy texture that many describe as rubbery-crunchy. It grows wild on logs of koa and kukui trees in Hawaii, typically on fallen or dying tree branches, often appearing after rain. It's known for its ability to absorb flavors when cooked and is commonly added to soups and stir-fries. It's a staple in Hawaii's Asian-influenced cuisine and is essentially the same category of mushroom used as "wood ear" or "cloud ear" in Chinese and Japanese cooking (sometimes called kikurage).

Maitake mushrooms (Grifola frondosa) are a type of edible mushroom native to Japan, China, and North America, where they grow wild at the base of oak, maple, and elm trees. Earthy, rich, and savory, often described as woodsy with a slightly peppery note. They have a nice meaty texture when cooked, similar to other polypore mushrooms. Popular in Japanese and other Asian cuisines — sautéed, roasted, added to soups, stir-fries, or used in broths. Their frilly texture crisps up nicely when roasted or pan-fried.

The mushroom commonly sold as "chestnut mushroom" is typically Pholiota adiposa (sometimes marketed varieties are hybrids/cultivars developed for the table), native to East Asia and popularized by Japanese cultivators.
The SHIITAKE (Lentinula edodes) is an edible mushroom native to East Asia, which is cultivated and consumed in many Asian countries.
PLEUROTUS OSTREATUS, the oyster mushroom, is a common edible mushroom.

"Cloud ear" (also called wood ear, black fungus, or mù'ěr 木耳 in Chinese) refers to mushrooms in the genus Auricularia — most commonly Auricularia auricula-judae or Auricularia cornea. They're a type of jelly fungus that grows on decaying or living wood, especially elder, beech, and other broadleaf trees. Cloud ears are prized more for their texture than flavor — they're crunchy, slightly gelatinous, and almost cartilaginous when cooked, but have very little taste of their own. That makes them great at soaking up other flavors in a dish.

"Pepeao" is a Hawaiian word — it literally means "ear," and it's used in Hawaii to refer to a type of jelly fungus (wood ear mushroom, genus Auricularia) because of its ear-shaped, rubbery cap. It grows on dead or decaying wood and is edible, often used in soups and stir-fries, similar to how "wood ear" or "cloud ear" mushrooms are used in Chinese cuisine.

A TRUFFLE is the fruiting body of a subterranean ascomycete fungus, predominantly one of the many species of the genus Tuber. In addition to Tuber, many other genera of fungi are classified as truffles including Geopora, Peziza, Choiromyces, Leucangium, and over a hundred others.

Mortierella alpina oil is derived from a soil-dwelling filamentous fungus, first isolated and studied for its lipid content in various regions worldwide, including Japan, China, and Europe, where it is produced industrially through fermentation. The refined oil is essentially flavorless and odorless, making it unobtrusive when blended into other products. It is primarily used as an additive in infant formula, nutritional supplements, and functional foods across global markets, valued for standardized quality and non-animal, non-fish origin. Nutritionally, it is notable for its high concentration of arachidonic acid, an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid also naturally present in human breast milk and various animal tissues.
QUORN is a meat substitute product originating in the UK and sold primarily in Europe, but also available in 19 countries.
Fish are gill-bearing aquatic craniate animals that lack limbs with digits.

Flat fish are a group of fish that live and swim mostly on the ocean floor, and their most striking feature is that their bodies are flattened sideways (laterally compressed) so they end up lying and swimming on one side rather than upright.
Fish, flatfish (flounder and sole species), raw
ROCKFISH is a common term for several species of fish, referring to their tendency to hide among rocks.
The Alaska pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus) is a marine fish species of the cod family Gadidae.
The European anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus) is a forage fish somewhat related to the herring.

Mahi-mahi is a species of fish, it's sometimes called "dolphinfish," but it's unrelated to dolphins. It's a large, colorful saltwater fish found in warm and temperate waters around the world, known for its firm, lean, mildly sweet white-to-pinkish flesh. Flavor and texture: Mild, slightly sweet flavor with a firm, meaty texture — often compared to swordfish or tuna, but lighter and less oily.

Milkfish (Chanos chanos) is a mild-flavored, silvery fish that's a staple food in parts of Southeast Asia, especially the Philippines, Indonesia, and Taiwan. Texture and flavor: The flesh is soft, slightly fatty, and has a mild taste that takes on marinades and seasonings well. It's notoriously bony, with many small, fine bones running through the flesh. This has led to specialty products like "boneless milkfish," where the bones are removed before selling.

"Anglerfish" is a broad term for an order of fish (Lophiiformes) known for using a fleshy growth on their head like a fishing lure to attract prey. The fish sold as "monkfish" in seafood markets typically refers to species in the genus Lophius — like the American anglerfish (Lophius americanus) or European anglerfish (Lophius piscatorius) — which live on the seafloor in relatively shallow coastal waters. Monkfish is prized in cooking mostly for its tail meat, which is the part typically sold and eaten. Texture and flavor: It has a firm, dense, meaty texture — often compared to lobster — with a mild, slightly sweet flavor. This has earned it the nickname "poor man's lobster."

The Atlantic wolffish (Anarhichas lupus), also known as the seawolf, Atlantic catfish, ocean catfish, devil fish, wolf eel (the common name for its Pacific relative), woof or sea cat, is a marine fish of the wolffish family Anarhichadidae.
Bar ou loup de l'Atlantique, cru
The blue whiting, Micromesistius poutassou, one of the two species in the genus Micromesistius in the cod family, is common in the northeast Atlantic Ocean from Morocco to Iceland and Spitsbergen

Bluefish (Pomatomus saltatrix) is a species of saltwater fish commonly eaten as food, especially along the Atlantic coasts of the US, and also found in various other parts of the world. Flavor and texture: It has a stronger, more "fishy" flavor than mild white fish like cod or tilapia. The flesh is oily/fatty (similar in that regard to mackerel or salmon), which gives it a rich taste but also means it spoils faster and is best cooked fresh.

Burbot (Lota lota) is a freshwater fish — and actually the only member of the cod family (Gadidae) that lives entirely in fresh water rather than the ocean. It's edible and considered quite good eating — sometimes nicknamed "poor man's lobster" because its liver and flesh are prized by some anglers, especially for winter ice-fishing.

Butterfish is the common name for a couple of different fish species, most notably: Escolar (Lepidocybium flavobrunneum) — sometimes marketed as "butterfish," this deep-sea fish has an extremely high oil content that gives it a rich, buttery texture and mouthfeel, hence the name. It's popular in sushi restaurants (sometimes mislabeled as "white tuna"); American butterfish (Peprilus triacanthus) — a smaller, silvery fish found along the U.S. Atlantic coast.

American butterfish (Peprilus triacanthus) is a small, deep-bodied fish from the northwest Atlantic, ranging from Labrador down to Florida's Gulf coast. Flavor and texture: It has soft, delicate, oily flesh with a mild, sweet flavor — the "butter" in the name comes from that rich, tender texture rather than any actual buttery taste. The flesh is white and flakes easily when cooked.

Die Lodde oder der Kapelan (Mallotus villosus) ist ein kleiner Fisch aus der Familie der Stinte, der in großen Schwärmen im Arktischen Ozean lebt. Die Weibchen werden hauptsächlich wegen ihres Rogens gefangen, der im Handel als „Capelinrogen“ oder „Isländischer Kaviar“ angeboten wird.

The capelin or caplin (Mallotus villosus) is a small forage fish of the smelt family found in the North Atlantic, North Pacific, and Arctic oceans. Commercialement, le capelan est utilisé comme produit alimentaire, et dans l'industrie des huiles de poisson. Sa chair a un goût agréable, ressemblant à celle du hareng. Les œufs de capelan ("masago") sont des produits alimentaires coûteux.
Mallotus villosus, le capelan, est un petit poisson des océans Atlantique et Glacial Arctique.

De lodde (Mallotus villosus) is de enige vertegenwoordiger van het monotypische geslacht Mallotus en een straalvinnige vis uit de familie van de spieringen (Osmeridae). De lodde is voor de beroepsvisserij van groot belang. Het kuit van de lodde is een delicatesse. In Nederland wordt deze echter als imitatie kaviaar verkocht.

Carp is a freshwater fish that's been eaten by humans for thousands of years — it's actually one of the oldest farmed food fish in the world, with cultivation going back to ancient China. Taste and texture: Mild, slightly sweet, and somewhat earthy or "muddy" tasting, especially if it comes from murky water. Farm-raised carp raised in cleaner water tends to taste better. The flesh is firm but has a lot of small bones, similar to other freshwater fish like pike.

Cisco is a freshwater whitefish in the genus Coregonus, found mainly in the Great Lakes and other cold lakes across North America (and some in Europe/Asia too). It's related to salmon and trout. Cisco  has a mild, delicate flavor — similar to other whitefish, slightly sweet. The texture is tender, flaky, fine-textured flesh — fairly delicate, can fall apart easily if overcooked.

Cusk (Brosme brosme) is a bottom-dwelling fish in the cod family (Gadidae), found in the cold waters of the North Atlantic — off the coasts of New England, Atlantic Canada, and northern Europe. Cusk has firm, white flesh similar to cod or haddock, and is prized by some for its mild flavor. It's often sold fresh or used in chowders.

Der Nilbarsch (Lates niloticus), in Deutschland als Speisefisch meist Viktoriabarsch genannt, ist ein Süßwasser-Raubfisch aus der Familie der Riesenbarsche (Latidae). Er kommt im tropischen und subtropischen Afrika in allen bedeutenden Flusssystemen vor.

The Nile perch (Lates niloticus), also known as the African snook, Goliath perch, Giant lates or the Victoria perch, is a species of freshwater fish in family Latidae of order Perciformes. It is widespread throughout much of the Afrotropical realm.
La perca del Nilo (Lates niloticus) es un pez de la familia Latidae.

Lates niloticus, conosciuto comunemente come persico del Nilo o persico africano, è un pesce d'acqua dolce appartenente alla famiglia Latidae.
De nijlbaars of Victoriabaars (Lates niloticus) is een soort van zoetwatervis uit de familie van de reuzenbaarzen
A perca-do-nilo (Lates niloticus) é um peixe da família dos Latidae.
Der Flussbarsch (Perca fluviatilis), am Bodensee Kretzer, in der Schweiz auch Egli genannt, ist ein in ganz Europa vorkommender Süßwasserfisch.

The European perch (Perca fluviatilis), also known as the common perch, redfin perch, big-scaled redfin, English perch, Eurasian perch, Eurasian river perch, Hatch or in Anglophone parts of Europe, simply the perch, is a predatory species of the freshwater perch native to Europe and northern Asia.
La perca o perca de río (Perca fluviatilis) es una especie de pez de la familia Percidae muy abundante en los ríos y lagos de casi toda Europa central y occidental.
La perche commune, perche franche ou encore perche française en France (Perca fluviatilis) est une espèce de poissons d'eau douce.
Il pesce persico (Perca fluviatilis), conosciuto comunemente in Italia come persico reale o semplicemente persico, è un pesce di acqua dolce.
De baars (Perca fluviatilis) is een vis uit de vissenfamilie echte baarzen, die in de Benelux inheems voorkomt.
A Perca fluviatilis é um peixe da família Percidae. Ocorre em rios da Europa e da Ásia.
Der Europäische Wolfsbarsch oder auch Seebarsch (Dicentrarchus labrax) ist ein Fisch aus der Familie der Wolfsbarsche.
The European bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) is a primarily ocean-going fish native to the waters off Europe's western and southern and Africa's northern coasts.
La lubina, lobina, róbalo, robalo5 o robaliza (Dicentrarchus labrax) es una especie de pez perciforme de la familia Moronidae.

Le bar commun ou bar européen (Dicentrarchus labrax), surnommé loup ou perche de mer, est une espèce de poissons principalement marins qui entrent parfois en eau saumâtre et en eau douce, appartenant à la famille des moronidés.

Dicentrarchus labrax nota comunemente come spigola (nell'Italia peninsulare e insulare) o branzino (prevalentemente nell'Italia settentrionale), è un pesce osseo marino e d'acqua salmastra della famiglia Moronidae.
De Europese zeebaars of zeebaars (Dicentrarchus labrax) is een straalvinnige vis uit de familie van Moronidae.

Dicentrarchus labrax é uma espécie de peixe da família Moronidae de tons acinzentados. Vulgarmente conhecido em Portugal por robalo e robalete, é muito apreciado na culinária portuguesa e de outros países europeus.

Morone saxatilis, gelegentlich als Felsenbarsch bezeichnet, ist ein Fisch aus der Familie der Wolfsbarsche.

The striped bass (Morone saxatilis), also called the Atlantic striped bass, striper, linesider, rock or rockfish, is an anadromous perciform fish of the family Moronidae found primarily along the Atlantic coast of North America.

Sablefish is a deep-water fish found in the North Pacific, from the Bering Sea down to Baja California. Flavor and texture: Rich, buttery, almost melt-in-your-mouth texture, thanks to a very high fat content; Mild, slightly sweet flavor — less "fishy" than many other fish; Large, silky white flakes. Very high in omega-3 fatty acids, even more than salmon per serving

Scup is a small saltwater fish found along the Atlantic coast of North America, from Nova Scotia down to Florida, though it's most abundant from Cape Cod to Cape Hatteras. Flavor and texture: Mild, slightly sweet white flesh, similar in character to other porgies or small snappers. It's a lean fish.

Taste and texture: Mild, sweet, and slightly nutty flavor; Firm, white, flaky flesh; Often compared to red snapper, black drum, or grouper; Because it eats mostly shellfish, crabs, and barnacles, some people say the diet gives it a faintly sweet, "crab-like" undertone

A small saltwater fish common along the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Spot has mild, sweet, flaky white flesh. It's popular in Southern U.S. cooking — often pan-fried or deep-fried whole (scaled and gutted), since the bones are easy to work around once cooked. It's a favorite at fish fries in the Carolinas, Georgia, and along the Gulf Coast.

Tilapia is one of the most widely farmed and eaten fish in the world — a mild, freshwater (or brackish-water) fish that's become a staple in supermarkets and restaurants globally. Flavor and texture: Mild, slightly sweet taste with no strong "fishy" flavor; Firm, flaky white flesh; Because it's so neutral-tasting, it takes on seasonings, marinades, and sauces well — which is a big part of its popularity

Tilefish is a type of saltwater fish found mainly in the western Atlantic Ocean, from the northeastern U.S. down through the Gulf of Mexico. There are a few species, but the most commonly eaten ones are golden tilefish (also called "white tilefish" in markets) and blueline tilefish. Flavor and texture: Mild, sweet flavor with firm, moist flesh — often compared to a cross between lobster and crab in taste, which is why it's sometimes nicknamed "poor man's lobster." The texture holds up well to various cooking methods. Cooking methods: It works well baked, roasted, pan-seared, grilled, or poached. The skin can be crisped up nicely in a pan. It's popular in Japanese cuisine too, where it's called amadai and often prepared with the scales left on and fried until crispy.

Swordfish is a large, fast-swimming ocean fish (Xiphias gladius) known for the long, flat, sword-like bill it uses to slash at prey. As food, it's prized for a few distinct qualities: Texture and flavor: The flesh is firm, meaty, and dense — often compared to a good steak more than to flakier white fish. The flavor is mild but slightly rich, with a subtle sweetness; Cut and cooking: It's usually sold as thick steaks rather than fillets, since the loin is large. It grills, broils, or pan-sears very well, and holds up on skewers (it's a common choice for kebabs); Fat content: It's a moderately fatty fish, which helps keep it moist during high-heat cooking like grilling — unlike very lean white fish that dry out easily.
